groups:
- name: node.rules
  interval: 1m
  rules:
  - alert: InstanceDown
    expr: up == 0
    for: 5m
    labels:
      severity: critical
    annotations:
      summary: "Instance {{ $labels.instance }} down"
      description: "{{ $labels.instance }} of job {{ $labels.job }} has been down for more than 5 minutes."
      runbook_url: https://runbooks.example.com/node/instance-down

  - alert: HostOutOfMemory
    expr: (node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes / node_memory_MemTotal_bytes * 100 < 10) * on(instance) group_left (nodename) node_uname_info{nodename=~".+"}
    for: 2m
    labels: { severity: warning }
    annotations:
      summary: Host out of memory (instance {{ $labels.instance }})
      description: "Node memory is filling up (< 10% left)\n  VALUE = {{ $value }}\n  LABELS = {{ $labels }}"

  - alert: HostHighCpuLoad
    expr: |
      sum by (instance) (avg by (mode, instance) (rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode!="idle"}[2m]))) > 0.8
      and on (instance)
      node_load5 > 4
    for: 10m
    labels:
      severity:   warning
      team: infra
    annotations:
      summary: 'Host high CPU load (instance {{ $labels.instance }})'

- name: storefront.slo
  rules:
    - record: job:http_requests:rate5m
      expr: sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
    - record: job:http_errors:ratio_rate5m
      expr: >
        sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[5m]))
        /
        sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
    - alert: StorefrontErrorBudgetBurn
      expr: job:http_errors:ratio_rate5m{job="storefront"} > (14.4 * (1 - 0.999))
      for: 2m
      labels:
        severity: page
        slo: availability
      annotations:
        summary: Storefront is burning its error budget 14.4x faster than allowed
        description: >-
          The 5 minute error ratio for {{ $labels.job }} is {{ $value | humanizePercentage }},
          which would exhaust the monthly error budget in roughly two days if it continues.
          Check recent deploys first, then the database and payment provider dashboards.

_Tidy data verbs for pandas, without the magic._

tidyframe gives you a small set of composable, well-named functions (`select`, `filter_rows`, `mutate`, `summarise`, `pivot_longer`, `pivot_wider`) that work on plain
`pandas.DataFrame` objects. There is no custom DataFrame subclass, no monkey patching and no
global state, so it plays nicely with the rest of the scientific Python ecosystem.

Installation
------------

    pip install tidyframe

or, with the optional [Arrow](https://arrow.apache.org/) backend:

    pip install "tidyframe[arrow]"

Quick start
-----------

```python
import pandas as pd
import tidyframe as tf

df = pd.read_csv("penguins.csv")

(
    df
    .pipe(tf.filter_rows, lambda d: d.species != "Gentoo")
    .pipe(tf.mutate, bill_ratio=lambda d: d.bill_length_mm / d.bill_depth_mm)
    .pipe(tf.summarise, by="species", mean_ratio=("bill_ratio", "mean"))
)
```

Why another library?
--------------------

There are several excellent projects in this space -- [siuba], [dplython] (unmaintained) and [polars] (a different DataFrame library altogether) -- but each of them either wraps the
DataFrame in its own type or relies on operator overloading tricks that confuse type checkers and IDEs.
tidyframe makes different trade-offs:

+ every verb is a plain function with a docstring and type hints
+ verbs never mutate their input
+ errors mention the column names you actually passed, e.g. ``KeyError: 'bill_lenght_mm' (did you mean 'bill_length_mm'?)``

2.1 | 3.9 - 3.12 | security fixes only

   python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
   pip install -e ".[dev]"

4. Open a pull request. A maintainer will usually respond within a week.

# @acme/tiny-fetch [![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@acme/tiny-fetch.svg?style=flat-square)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@acme/tiny-fetch) [![bundle size](https://img.shields.io/bundlephobia/minzip/@acme/tiny-fetch?style=flat-square)](https://bundlephobia.com/package/@acme/tiny-fetch)

> A 1.2 kB wrapper around `fetch` with retries, timeouts, and JSON helpers. Works in browsers, Node 18+, Deno and Bun.

## Install

```bash
npm i @acme/tiny-fetch
# or
pnpm add @acme/tiny-fetch
```

## Usage
```js
import { get, post } from '@acme/tiny-fetch'

const user = await get('/api/users/42', { timeout: 5_000, retries: 2 })
await post('/api/events', { type: 'click', target: '#buy' })
```

## API

### `get(url, options?)`
### `post(url, body, options?)`

Options:

|option|type|default|description|
|-|-|-|-|
|`timeout`|`number`|`10000`|Milliseconds before the request is aborted with a `TimeoutError`.|
|`retries`|`number`|`0`|How many times to retry on network errors and `5xx` responses. Uses exponential backoff with full jitter (base 200 ms, max 5 s).|
|`headers`|`Record<string, string>`|`{}`|Extra headers merged into the defaults.|
|`signal`|`AbortSignal`|—|Your own abort signal; combined with the timeout signal.|
|`parse`|`'json' \| 'text' \| 'blob' \| false`|`'json'`|How to parse the response body.|

__Errors__ are thrown as `HttpError` (with `status`, `statusText` and the parsed `body`) or `TimeoutError`. Both extend `Error`, so `instanceof` checks work as expected even across realms as long as you import them from the same copy of the package.

## Browser support

Any browser that supports `fetch` and `AbortController`:  Chrome 66+, Firefox 57+, Safari 12.1+, Edge 79+. For older browsers you'll need a polyfill such as [whatwg-fetch](https://github.com/github/fetch) together with [abortcontroller-polyfill](https://github.com/mo/abortcontroller-polyfill).

## Comparison

| | tiny-fetch | ky | axios |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Size (min+gz) | 1.2 kB | 4.1 kB | 13.6 kB |
| Retries | ✓ | ✓ | plugin |
| Interceptors |✗|✓ (hooks)|✓|
| Node < 18 | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ |

## License
MIT © ACME

# Changelog
All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.

The format is based on [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/),
and this project adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html).

## [Unreleased]
### Added
- `--exclude` can now be given multiple times ([#231](https://github.com/example/gitpulse/pull/231)).
- New `bus-factor` sub-command.

### Changed
- Bumped MSRV to 1.74.
-  The default time window changed from 30 to 90 days because 30 days turned out to be too noisy for most repositories we tested with.

## [0.9.2] - 2026-09-14
### Fixed
- Crash when a commit has no author email (#228).
- `--json` output no longer contains trailing commas in the `files` array when `--top` is used together with `--exclude`, which made some strict JSON parsers (looking at you, older versions of `jq`) reject the output.

## [0.9.1] - 2026-08-30
### Fixed
* Windows: paths with backslashes are now normalised before matching `--exclude` globs.

### Security
* Updated `gix` to pick up an upstream fix for a path traversal issue in checkout handling.

## [0.9.0] - 2026-07-02
### Added
- Pull request lead time for GitLab merge requests.
- `--csv` output.
### Changed
- **Breaking:** renamed `--author` to `--by-author` for consistency with `--by-directory`.
### Deprecated
- The `GITPULSE_GH_TOKEN` environment variable; use `GITPULSE_TOKEN` instead.
### Removed
- Support for git < 2.30.

## [0.8.0] - 2026-03-11

### Added

- Initial support for `.mailmap`.
- Colours! Can be disabled with `--no-color` or the `NO_COLOR` environment variable.


## 0.1.0 - 2025-11-02
- First public release.

Changelog
=========

Version 3.2.0
-------------

Released 2026-05-04

* Added ``Config.from_env`` which reads settings from environment
  variables prefixed with ``APP_``. :issue:`512`
* The ``--reload`` flag now watches template files as well as Python
  files.
* Dropped support for Python 3.8, which reached end of life in October 2024.
+ Fixed a race condition in the reloader on macOS where file events were occasionally delivered twice, causing the server to restart in a loop until the terminal was closed.

Version 3.1.1
-------------
Released 2026-02-17

*   Fix ``TypeError`` when ``url_for`` was called with ``_external=True``
    outside of a request context.  [#498][]
*   Docs: clarify the order in which configuration sources are merged.


Version 3.1.0
-------------

_Released 2025-12-01_

- **Highlights**
  - New `app.cli.group()` decorator for nesting command groups
  - Faster startup (lazy import of `jinja2`, roughly 40 ms saved)
- **Other changes**
  - `send_file` sets `Content-Disposition` correctly for non-ASCII filenames (RFC 6266 / RFC 5987 encoding)
  - Removed the long-deprecated `json_encoder` attribute.

Version 3.0.0
=============

**This is a major release with breaking changes. Please read the [upgrade guide][upgrading] before updating.**

* Minimum Python version is now 3.9.
* The default session interface signs cookies with SHA-256 instead of SHA-1. Existing sessions are invalidated on upgrade.
* ``before_first_request`` has been removed. Use the app factory pattern
instead (see [#401][]).

[#401]: https://github.com/example/flaskish/pull/401

|`parse`|`'json' \| 'text' \| 'blob' \| false`|`'json'`|How to parse the response body.|

__Errors__ are thrown as `HttpError` (with `status`, `statusText` and the parsed `body`) or `TimeoutError`. Both extend `Error`, so `instanceof` checks work as expected even across realms as long as you import them from the same copy of the package.

## Browser support

Any browser that supports `fetch` and `AbortController`:  Chrome 66+, Firefox 57+, Safari 12.1+, Edge 79+. For older browsers you'll need a polyfill such as [whatwg-fetch](https://github.com/github/fetch) together with [abortcontroller-polyfill](https://github.com/mo/abortcontroller-polyfill).

## Comparison

| | tiny-fetch | ky | axios |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Size (min+gz) | 1.2 kB | 4.1 kB | 13.6 kB |
| Retries | ✓ | ✓ | plugin |
| Interceptors |✗|✓ (hooks)|✓|
| Node < 18 | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ |

Contributing to Widgets
=======================

First of all: thank you for considering a contribution!   Widgets is maintained by a small group of volunteers and every bug report, docs fix and pull request genuinely helps.

The notes below describe how we like to work. They are guidelines rather than hard rules -- use your judgement, and if something here seems wrong or outdated, open a pull request against this file.

#### Table Of Contents

[Code of Conduct](#code-of-conduct)

[I just have a question!](#i-just-have-a-question)

[How Can I Contribute?](#how-can-i-contribute)
  * [Reporting Bugs](#reporting-bugs)
  * [Suggesting Enhancements](#suggesting-enhancements)
  * [Your First Code Contribution](#your-first-code-contribution)
  * [Pull Requests](#pull-requests)

[Styleguides](#styleguides)
  * [Git Commit Messages](#git-commit-messages)
  * [Python Styleguide](#python-styleguide)
  * [Documentation Styleguide](#documentation-styleguide)

## Code of Conduct

Everyone taking part in this project is expected to follow the [Widgets Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). Please report unacceptable behaviour to [conduct@example.com](mailto:conduct@example.com).

## I just have a question!

> **Note:** please don't open an issue just to ask a question -- you'll get a faster answer in one of the places below.

* [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/acme/widgets/discussions), where most of the maintainers hang out
* The [FAQ](https://widgets.example.com/faq), which covers the questions we get asked most often
* The `#widgets` channel on the community chat server

## How Can I Contribute?

### Reporting Bugs

Before filing a bug, search the [existing issues](https://github.com/acme/widgets/issues?q=is%3Aissue) -- somebody may already have reported it, and a :+1: reaction on an existing issue helps us prioritise. If you do open a new one, fill in the issue template as completely as you can.

#### What makes a good bug report?

Bugs are tracked as GitHub issues. When you create one, please:

* **Use a clear and descriptive title.**
* **List the exact steps to reproduce the problem.** Include the command you ran, the relevant part of your `widgets.yml`, and the full error message or traceback.
* **Describe what you expected to happen**, and what happened instead.
* **Include your environment**: OS, Python version, and the output of `widgets --version`.
* If the problem started after an upgrade, tell us the last version that worked.

### Suggesting Enhancements

Enhancement suggestions are tracked as GitHub issues too. Explain the problem you are trying to solve *before* describing the solution you have in mind; there is often more than one way to address a use case, and the best one is not always the first one that comes to mind.

### Your First Code Contribution

Not sure where to start? Have a look at these labels:

1. [Good first issues][good-first] - small, well-defined issues that should only need a few lines of code and a test.
2. [Help wanted][help-wanted] - somewhat larger issues where we would welcome outside help.
3) Documentation issues - typos, unclear wording, missing examples.

#### Local development

```shell
git clone https://github.com/acme/widgets && cd widgets
make dev        # creates .venv and installs pre-commit hooks
make test       # runs pytest with coverage
make docs-serve # live-reloading docs on http://127.0.0.1:8000
```

### Pull Requests

A few things that make reviews go smoothly:

- Keep pull requests focused. One bug fix or feature per PR is much easier to review than a mixed bag.
- Add or update tests for any behaviour change.
- Update the documentation if you change user-facing behaviour.
- Add an entry to `CHANGELOG.md` under *Unreleased*.

Please follow these steps to have your contribution considered by the maintainers:

1. Fill in [the pull request template](PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md)
2. Follow the [styleguides](#styleguides)
3. After you submit your pull request, check that all status checks pass <details><summary>What if a check fails for reasons unrelated to my change?</summary>Leave a comment on the pull request saying so. A maintainer will take a look and re-run the job if it was a flaky test.</details>

## Styleguides

### Git Commit Messages

* Use the present tense ("Add feature" not "Added feature")
* Use the imperative mood ("Move cursor to..." not "Moves cursor to...")
* Limit the first line to 72 characters or less
* Reference issues and pull requests liberally after the first line
* Consider starting the commit message with a [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) type:
    * `feat:` a new feature
    * `fix:` a bug fix
    * `docs:` documentation only changes
    * `refactor:` a code change that neither fixes a bug nor adds a feature

### Python Styleguide

All Python code is formatted with `ruff format` and linted with `ruff check`.  Type hints are required for all public functions.

### Documentation Styleguide

* Use [Markdown](https://daringfireball.net/projects/markdown).
* Wrap prose at 100 columns; one sentence per line is also fine.
* Reference functions with backticks: `widgets.render()`.

[good-first]: https://github.com/acme/widgets/issues?q=is%3Aopen+is%3Aissue+label%3A%22good+first+issue%22
[help-wanted]:https://github.com/acme/widgets/issues?q=is%3Aopen+is%3Aissue+label%3A%22help+wanted%22

Code of Conduct
===============

*Last updated: March 2026*

## Why we have this document ##

The `widgets` community is made up of people from many countries, backgrounds and levels of experience.  We want every one of them to feel safe asking questions, reporting bugs, reviewing code and disagreeing with each other -- and we want disagreements to stay about the work, never about the person.

This document describes the behaviour we expect, the behaviour we will
not accept, and what happens when someone crosses the line. It applies in every
project space: the issue tracker, pull requests, discussions, the chat server,
video calls, and any event where someone is representing the project.

## What we expect ##

* Be patient with newcomers. Everybody was new once, and "read the docs" is not an answer unless you also link to the part of the docs you mean.
* Assume good intent, but notice impact. If someone tells you a comment of yours hurt, believe them, apologise, and adjust.
* Give feedback on code, not on people. "This loop is O(n²)" is useful; "who wrote this garbage" is not.
- Credit others for their work and ideas.
- Respect people's time: keep discussions on topic and move long tangents to a separate thread.

## What we will not accept

1. Harassment of any kind, in public or in private messages.
2. Insults, slurs, or demeaning jokes about anyone's identity, including (but not limited to) gender, sexual orientation, disability, ethnicity, religion, age or appearance.
3. Sharing someone's personal information without their explicit permission ("doxxing").
4. Sustained disruption of discussions, e.g. repeatedly derailing threads or spamming.
5. Encouraging any of the above.

## Reporting

If you experience or witness unacceptable behaviour, email **conduct@example.com**. The address reaches a small group of maintainers (currently three people, listed in [MAINTAINERS.md](MAINTAINERS.md)); if your report concerns one of them, they will be excluded from handling it.

You will get an acknowledgement within 72 hours.   Reports are kept confidential; we will only share details with your permission or where required by law.

## Enforcement

Depending on the severity, maintainers may:

- send a private, written warning;
- ask for a public apology;
- temporarily ban the person from project spaces (typically 30 days);
- permanently ban the person.

Decisions can be appealed once, by email, within 14 days.


## Attribution

Parts of this document were inspired by the [Contributor Covenant](https://www.contributor-covenant.org), version 2.1, and the [Django Code of Conduct](https://www.djangoproject.com/conduct/).

# Security Policy

## Supported Versions

Use this section to tell people about which versions of your project are
currently being supported with security updates.

| Version | Supported          |
| ------- | ------------------ |
| 5.1.x   | :white_check_mark: |
| 5.0.x   | :x:                |
| 4.0.x   | :white_check_mark: |
| < 4.0   | :x:                |

## Reporting a Vulnerability

**Please do not report security vulnerabilities through public GitHub issues, discussions, or pull requests.**

Instead, please report them via [GitHub's private vulnerability reporting](https://github.com/acme/widgets/security/advisories/new) or send an email to security@example.com. If possible, encrypt your message with our PGP key; the fingerprint is `4F2B 9A1C 77D0 3E5A 8B21  C0DE 1234 5678 9ABC DEF0`.

Please include as much of the following information as you can, to help us understand the nature and scope of the issue:

  * Type of issue (e.g. buffer overflow, SQL injection, cross-site scripting, etc.)
  * Full paths of source file(s) related to the manifestation of the issue
  * The location of the affected source code (tag/branch/commit or direct URL)
  * Any special configuration required to reproduce the issue
  * Step-by-step instructions to reproduce the issue
  * Proof-of-concept or exploit code (if possible)
  * Impact of the issue, including how an attacker might exploit it

You should receive a response within 48 hours. If for some reason you do not, please follow up via email to ensure we received your original message.

## Disclosure policy
When we receive a security bug report, we will:
1. Confirm the problem and determine the affected versions.
2. Audit code to find any potential similar problems.
3. Prepare fixes for all releases still under maintenance. These fixes will be released as fast as possible.

We credit reporters in the release notes unless they ask us not to.

# Getting started

This guide walks you through installing **Widgets**, creating a project and rendering your first dashboard. It assumes you are comfortable with the command line and have Python 3.10 or newer installed. If you have never used a virtual environment before, read [the Python packaging guide on virtual environments](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/guides/installing-using-pip-and-virtual-environments/#create-and-use-virtual-environments) first -- it will save you some headaches later.

!!! note
    Widgets 3.x requires Python 3.10+. If you are stuck on an older interpreter, pin `widgets<3`.

## 1. Install

=== "pip"

    ```bash
    python -m pip install widgets
    ```

=== "conda"

    ```bash
    conda install -c conda-forge widgets
    ```

=== "uv"

    ```bash
    uv add widgets
    ```

Check that the installation worked:

```console
$ widgets --version
widgets 3.4.1
```

## 2. Create a project

```bash
widgets init my-dashboard
cd my-dashboard
```

This creates the following layout:

```text
my-dashboard/
├── widgets.yml        # project configuration
├── dashboards/
│   └── overview.yml
└── data/
    └── sample.csv
```

!!! tip "Use version control"
    Run `git init` right away. Dashboards are plain YAML files, so diffs are easy to review and you can roll back mistakes.

??? warning "Windows users"
    If `widgets` is not found after installation, the Scripts directory of your Python installation is probably not on your `PATH`.
    Use `py -m widgets` instead, or re-run the installer and tick *Add Python to PATH*.

## 3. Render the dashboard

1. Start the development server:

        widgets serve --reload

2. Open <http://localhost:8050> in your browser.
3. Edit `dashboards/overview.yml` -- for example change the `title` -- and watch the page reload.
10. When you are happy, build a static version with `widgets build --out site/`.

!!! danger
    Never run `widgets serve` on a public interface. It is a development server with *no* authentication.

## Next steps

* Learn about [layouts](../user-guide/layouts.md) and [themes](../user-guide/themes.md)
* Connect a real [data source](../user-guide/data-sources/index.md)
* Browse the [gallery](https://widgets.example.com/gallery/){ .md-button }

Configuration reference
=======================

Widgets reads its configuration from `widgets.yml` in the project root[^1]. Every key can also be set through an environment variable: upper-case the dotted path, replace dots with double underscores and prefix it with `WIDGETS_`, e.g. `server.port` becomes `WIDGETS_SERVER__PORT`.

## Top-level keys

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | ---- | ------- | ----------- |
| `title` | string | `"Widgets"` | Shown in the browser tab and the navigation bar. |
| `theme` | string \| mapping | `default` | Either the name of a built-in theme (`default`, `dark`, `solarized`) or a mapping with `base` and `overrides`. |
| `server.host` | string | `127.0.0.1` | Interface to bind to. |
| `server.port` | integer | `8050` | |
| `cache.backend` | `memory` \| `redis` \| `disk` | `memory` | See [Caching](#caching). |
| `auth` | mapping | *none* | Authentication settings; when absent the server is unauthenticated[^2]. |

## Example

```yaml
title: Sales overview
theme:
  base: dark
  overrides:
    accent: "#ff6f61"
server:
  host: 0.0.0.0
  port: 8080
cache:
  backend: redis
  url: redis://localhost:6379/2
  ttl: 300
```

## Caching

Widgets caches query results keyed by the query text and its parameters.  With the `memory` backend the cache lives inside the server process and is lost on restart, which is fine for development but rarely what you want in production where you typically run several worker processes behind a load balancer and want them to share a cache.

The `redis` backend accepts any URL understood by [redis-py](https://redis-py.readthedocs.io/en/stable/connections.html#redis.Redis.from_url), including `rediss://` for TLS and `unix://` sockets.
The `disk` backend stores pickled results under `.widgets-cache/`; it is safe to delete that directory at any time.

### Cache invalidation

You can invalidate the cache:

- per data source, by bumping `cache.version` in the data source definition,
- globally, by running `widgets cache clear`, or
- programmatically through the REST endpoint `POST /api/cache/clear` (requires the `admin` role).

## Logging

Logging follows the standard library's [`logging.config.dictConfig`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.config.html#logging-config-dictschema) schema, so anything you can express there you can put under the `logging` key:

```yaml
logging:
  version: 1
  root: { level: INFO, handlers: [console] }
  handlers:
    console: { class: logging.StreamHandler, formatter: plain }
  formatters:
    plain: { format: "%(asctime)s %(levelname)-8s %(name)s: %(message)s" }
```

[^1]: Or the file passed with `--config`. Relative paths inside the file are resolved relative to the file itself, not the current working directory.
[^2]: Seriously, don't do that on the open internet.

Frequently Asked Questions
==========================

General
-------

### Is Widgets free?

Yes. Widgets is open source under the Apache 2.0 license. There is a hosted version, *Widgets Cloud*, which is a paid product, but everything in this repository is and will remain free.

### Who is behind it?
Widgets was started in 2019 by a small team at ACME and is now maintained by a group of volunteers and two full-time engineers. See the [governance page](governance.md).

Troubleshooting
---------------

### "Address already in use" when running `widgets serve`

Another process is listening on port 8050.  Either stop it or pick a different port:

    widgets serve --port 8051

On Linux you can find the culprit with `ss -ltnp | grep 8050`, on macOS with `lsof -iTCP:8050 -sTCP:LISTEN`.

### My dashboard is blank
> Check the browser console first. In nine out of ten cases a query failed and the error is logged there.
>
> If the console is clean, run the server with `--log-level debug` and look for lines starting with `query:`.
>> Tip: `widgets doctor` checks the most common misconfigurations automatically.

### The PDF export cuts off wide tables

This is a known limitation of the headless browser we use for printing. Workarounds, in order of preference:

1. switch the table to `layout: scroll`, which the exporter renders on multiple pages
1. reduce the font size with `print.font_scale: 0.8`
1. export as PNG instead

Roadmap
-------

Things we are working on for the next release:

- [x] Redis cache backend
- [x] Dark theme
- [ ] Row-level security for data sources
- [ ] Scheduled e-mail reports
  - [x] design doc
  - [ ] SMTP backend
  - [ ] templates
- [ ] ~~Excel export~~ (dropped, use CSV)

*Didn't find your question?* Ask in [Discussions](https://github.com/acme/widgets/discussions) or on the chat server; we're friendly.

# API reference #

The `widgets` Python API is __stable__ from version 3.0 on: anything documented on this page follows [semantic versioning](https://semver.org). Names starting with an underscore are _private_ and may change at any time.

## `widgets.Dashboard` ##

```python
class Dashboard(title: str, *, layout: Layout | None = None, theme: str = "default")
```

A container for widgets.

__Parameters__

* `title` -- shown above the dashboard.
* `layout` -- a `Layout` instance; defaults to a responsive 12-column grid.
* `theme` -- the name of a registered theme.

__Example__

```python
from widgets import Dashboard, Chart

dash = Dashboard("Sales")
dash.add(Chart.line(data="sales.csv", x="month", y="revenue"), row=0, col=0, width=8)
dash.serve()
```

### `Dashboard.add(widget, *, row, col, width=4, height=1)` ###
Adds a widget at the given grid position. Raises `LayoutError` if it overlaps another widget _and_ `allow_overlap` is false.

### `Dashboard.serve(host="127.0.0.1", port=8050, reload=False)` ###
Starts the development server. See [the CLI docs](cli.md#serve) for the equivalent command line flags.

## `widgets.Chart` ##

Factory functions: `Chart.line`, `Chart.bar`, `Chart.scatter`, `Chart.area`, `Chart.pie` (deprecated, use `Chart.donut`).

All factory functions accept the following keyword arguments:

Argument | Type | Description
:--|:--|:--
`data` | `str \| DataFrame \| DataSource` | Where the data comes from.
`x`, `y` | `str` | Column names.
`color` | `str \| None` | Column used for the colour encoding.
`title`| `str \| None` |
`tooltip` | `list[str]` | Columns shown on hover; defaults to `[x, y]`.

#### Deprecated: `Chart.pie` ####

> __Deprecated since 3.2:__ `Chart.pie` will be removed in 4.0. `Chart.donut(hole=0)` produces the same output.

## Exceptions ##

`WidgetsError`
: Base class for all exceptions raised by the library.

`LayoutError`
: Raised when widgets overlap or exceed the grid.

`DataSourceError`
: Raised when a data source cannot be reached. The original exception is available as `__cause__`.

Contributing to Widgets
=======================

First of all: thank you for considering a contribution!   Widgets is maintained by a small group of volunteers and every bug report, docs fix and pull request genuinely helps.

The notes below describe how we like to work. They are guidelines rather than hard rules -- use your judgement, and if something here seems wrong or outdated, open a pull request against this file.

#### Table Of Contents

[Code of Conduct](#code-of-conduct)

[I just have a question!](#i-just-have-a-question)

[How Can I Contribute?](#how-can-i-contribute)
  * [Reporting Bugs](#reporting-bugs)
  * [Suggesting Enhancements](#suggesting-enhancements)
  * [Your First Code Contribution](#your-first-code-contribution)
  * [Pull Requests](#pull-requests)

[Styleguides](#styleguides)
  * [Git Commit Messages](#git-commit-messages)
  * [Python Styleguide](#python-styleguide)
  * [Documentation Styleguide](#documentation-styleguide)

## Code of Conduct

Everyone taking part in this project is expected to follow the [Widgets Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). Please report unacceptable behaviour to [conduct@example.com](mailto:conduct@example.com).

## I just have a question!

> **Note:** please don't open an issue just to ask a question -- you'll get a faster answer in one of the places below.

* [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/acme/widgets/discussions), where most of the maintainers hang out
* The [FAQ](https://widgets.example.com/faq), which covers the questions we get asked most often
* The `#widgets` channel on the community chat server

## How Can I Contribute?

### Reporting Bugs

Before filing a bug, search the [existing issues](https://github.com/acme/widgets/issues?q=is%3Aissue) -- somebody may already have reported it, and a :+1: reaction on an existing issue helps us prioritise. If you do open a new one, fill in the issue template as completely as you can.

#### What makes a good bug report?

Bugs are tracked as GitHub issues. When you create one, please:

* **Use a clear and descriptive title.**
* **List the exact steps to reproduce the problem.** Include the command you ran, the relevant part of your `widgets.yml`, and the full error message or traceback.
* **Describe what you expected to happen**, and what happened instead.
* **Include your environment**: OS, Python version, and the output of `widgets --version`.
* If the problem started after an upgrade, tell us the last version that worked.

### Suggesting Enhancements

Enhancement suggestions are tracked as GitHub issues too. Explain the problem you are trying to solve *before* describing the solution you have in mind; there is often more than one way to address a use case, and the best one is not always the first one that comes to mind.

### Your First Code Contribution

Not sure where to start? Have a look at these labels:

1. [Good first issues][good-first] - small, well-defined issues that should only need a few lines of code and a test.
2. [Help wanted][help-wanted] - somewhat larger issues where we would welcome outside help.
3) Documentation issues - typos, unclear wording, missing examples.

#### Local development

```shell
git clone https://github.com/acme/widgets && cd widgets
make dev        # creates .venv and installs pre-commit hooks
make test       # runs pytest with coverage
make docs-serve # live-reloading docs on http://127.0.0.1:8000
```

### Pull Requests

A few things that make reviews go smoothly:

- Keep pull requests focused. One bug fix or feature per PR is much easier to review than a mixed bag.
- Add or update tests for any behaviour change.
- Update the documentation if you change user-facing behaviour.
- Add an entry to `CHANGELOG.md` under *Unreleased*.

Please follow these steps to have your contribution considered by the maintainers:

1. Fill in [the pull request template](PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md)
2. Follow the [styleguides](#styleguides)
3. After you submit your pull request, check that all status checks pass <details><summary>What if a check fails for reasons unrelated to my change?</summary>Leave a comment on the pull request saying so. A maintainer will take a look and re-run the job if it was a flaky test.</details>

## Styleguides

### Git Commit Messages

* Use the present tense ("Add feature" not "Added feature")
* Use the imperative mood ("Move cursor to..." not "Moves cursor to...")
* Limit the first line to 72 characters or less
* Reference issues and pull requests liberally after the first line
* Consider starting the commit message with a [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) type:
    * `feat:` a new feature
    * `fix:` a bug fix
    * `docs:` documentation only changes
    * `refactor:` a code change that neither fixes a bug nor adds a feature

### Python Styleguide

All Python code is formatted with `ruff format` and linted with `ruff check`.  Type hints are required for all public functions.

### Documentation Styleguide

* Use [Markdown](https://daringfireball.net/projects/markdown).
* Wrap prose at 100 columns; one sentence per line is also fine.
* Reference functions with backticks: `widgets.render()`.

[good-first]: https://github.com/acme/widgets/issues?q=is%3Aopen+is%3Aissue+label%3A%22good+first+issue%22
[help-wanted]:https://github.com/acme/widgets/issues?q=is%3Aopen+is%3Aissue+label%3A%22help+wanted%22

Code of Conduct
===============

*Last updated: March 2026*

## Why we have this document ##

The `widgets` community is made up of people from many countries, backgrounds and levels of experience.  We want every one of them to feel safe asking questions, reporting bugs, reviewing code and disagreeing with each other -- and we want disagreements to stay about the work, never about the person.

This document describes the behaviour we expect, the behaviour we will
not accept, and what happens when someone crosses the line. It applies in every
project space: the issue tracker, pull requests, discussions, the chat server,
video calls, and any event where someone is representing the project.

## What we expect ##

* Be patient with newcomers. Everybody was new once, and "read the docs" is not an answer unless you also link to the part of the docs you mean.
* Assume good intent, but notice impact. If someone tells you a comment of yours hurt, believe them, apologise, and adjust.
* Give feedback on code, not on people. "This loop is O(n²)" is useful; "who wrote this garbage" is not.
- Credit others for their work and ideas.
- Respect people's time: keep discussions on topic and move long tangents to a separate thread.

## What we will not accept

1. Harassment of any kind, in public or in private messages.
2. Insults, slurs, or demeaning jokes about anyone's identity, including (but not limited to) gender, sexual orientation, disability, ethnicity, religion, age or appearance.
3. Sharing someone's personal information without their explicit permission ("doxxing").
4. Sustained disruption of discussions, e.g. repeatedly derailing threads or spamming.
5. Encouraging any of the above.

## Reporting

If you experience or witness unacceptable behaviour, email **conduct@example.com**. The address reaches a small group of maintainers (currently three people, listed in [MAINTAINERS.md](MAINTAINERS.md)); if your report concerns one of them, they will be excluded from handling it.

You will get an acknowledgement within 72 hours.   Reports are kept confidential; we will only share details with your permission or where required by law.

## Enforcement

Depending on the severity, maintainers may:

- send a private, written warning;
- ask for a public apology;
- temporarily ban the person from project spaces (typically 30 days);
- permanently ban the person.

Decisions can be appealed once, by email, within 14 days.


## Attribution

Parts of this document were inspired by the [Contributor Covenant](https://www.contributor-covenant.org), version 2.1, and the [Django Code of Conduct](https://www.djangoproject.com/conduct/).

# Security Policy

## Supported Versions

Use this section to tell people about which versions of your project are
currently being supported with security updates.

| Version | Supported          |
| ------- | ------------------ |
| 5.1.x   | :white_check_mark: |
| 5.0.x   | :x:                |
| 4.0.x   | :white_check_mark: |
| < 4.0   | :x:                |

## Reporting a Vulnerability

**Please do not report security vulnerabilities through public GitHub issues, discussions, or pull requests.**

Instead, please report them via [GitHub's private vulnerability reporting](https://github.com/acme/widgets/security/advisories/new) or send an email to security@example.com. If possible, encrypt your message with our PGP key; the fingerprint is `4F2B 9A1C 77D0 3E5A 8B21  C0DE 1234 5678 9ABC DEF0`.

Please include as much of the following information as you can, to help us understand the nature and scope of the issue:

  * Type of issue (e.g. buffer overflow, SQL injection, cross-site scripting, etc.)
  * Full paths of source file(s) related to the manifestation of the issue
  * The location of the affected source code (tag/branch/commit or direct URL)
  * Any special configuration required to reproduce the issue
  * Step-by-step instructions to reproduce the issue
  * Proof-of-concept or exploit code (if possible)
  * Impact of the issue, including how an attacker might exploit it

You should receive a response within 48 hours. If for some reason you do not, please follow up via email to ensure we received your original message.

## Disclosure policy
When we receive a security bug report, we will:
1. Confirm the problem and determine the affected versions.
2. Audit code to find any potential similar problems.
3. Prepare fixes for all releases still under maintenance. These fixes will be released as fast as possible.

We credit reporters in the release notes unless they ask us not to.

tags: [ tutorial, beginner ]

# Getting started

This guide walks you through installing **Widgets**, creating a project and rendering your first dashboard. It assumes you are comfortable with the command line and have Python 3.10 or newer installed. If you have never used a virtual environment before, read [the Python packaging guide on virtual environments](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/guides/installing-using-pip-and-virtual-environments/#create-and-use-virtual-environments) first -- it will save you some headaches later.

!!! note
    Widgets 3.x requires Python 3.10+. If you are stuck on an older interpreter, pin `widgets<3`.

## 1. Install

=== "pip"

    ```bash
    python -m pip install widgets
    ```

=== "conda"

    ```bash
    conda install -c conda-forge widgets
    ```

=== "uv"

    ```bash
    uv add widgets
    ```

Check that the installation worked:

```console
$ widgets --version
widgets 3.4.1
```

## 2. Create a project

```bash
widgets init my-dashboard
cd my-dashboard
```

This creates the following layout:

```text
my-dashboard/
├── widgets.yml        # project configuration
├── dashboards/
│   └── overview.yml
└── data/
    └── sample.csv
```

!!! tip "Use version control"
    Run `git init` right away. Dashboards are plain YAML files, so diffs are easy to review and you can roll back mistakes.

??? warning "Windows users"
    If `widgets` is not found after installation, the Scripts directory of your Python installation is probably not on your `PATH`.
    Use `py -m widgets` instead, or re-run the installer and tick *Add Python to PATH*.

## 3. Render the dashboard

1. Start the development server:

        widgets serve --reload

2. Open <http://localhost:8050> in your browser.
3. Edit `dashboards/overview.yml` -- for example change the `title` -- and watch the page reload.
10. When you are happy, build a static version with `widgets build --out site/`.

!!! danger
    Never run `widgets serve` on a public interface. It is a development server with *no* authentication.

## Next steps

* Learn about [layouts](../user-guide/layouts.md) and [themes](../user-guide/themes.md)
* Connect a real [data source](../user-guide/data-sources/index.md)
* Browse the [gallery](https://widgets.example.com/gallery/){ .md-button }

Configuration reference
=======================

Widgets reads its configuration from `widgets.yml` in the project root[^1]. Every key can also be set through an environment variable: upper-case the dotted path, replace dots with double underscores and prefix it with `WIDGETS_`, e.g. `server.port` becomes `WIDGETS_SERVER__PORT`.

## Top-level keys

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | ---- | ------- | ----------- |
| `title` | string | `"Widgets"` | Shown in the browser tab and the navigation bar. |
| `theme` | string \| mapping | `default` | Either the name of a built-in theme (`default`, `dark`, `solarized`) or a mapping with `base` and `overrides`. |
| `server.host` | string | `127.0.0.1` | Interface to bind to. |
| `server.port` | integer | `8050` | |
| `cache.backend` | `memory` \| `redis` \| `disk` | `memory` | See [Caching](#caching). |
| `auth` | mapping | *none* | Authentication settings; when absent the server is unauthenticated[^2]. |

## Example

```yaml
title: Sales overview
theme:
  base: dark
  overrides:
    accent: "#ff6f61"
server:
  host: 0.0.0.0
  port: 8080
cache:
  backend: redis
  url: redis://localhost:6379/2
  ttl: 300
```

## Caching

Widgets caches query results keyed by the query text and its parameters.  With the `memory` backend the cache lives inside the server process and is lost on restart, which is fine for development but rarely what you want in production where you typically run several worker processes behind a load balancer and want them to share a cache.

The `redis` backend accepts any URL understood by [redis-py](https://redis-py.readthedocs.io/en/stable/connections.html#redis.Redis.from_url), including `rediss://` for TLS and `unix://` sockets.
The `disk` backend stores pickled results under `.widgets-cache/`; it is safe to delete that directory at any time.

### Cache invalidation

You can invalidate the cache:

- per data source, by bumping `cache.version` in the data source definition,
- globally, by running `widgets cache clear`, or
- programmatically through the REST endpoint `POST /api/cache/clear` (requires the `admin` role).

## Logging

Logging follows the standard library's [`logging.config.dictConfig`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.config.html#logging-config-dictschema) schema, so anything you can express there you can put under the `logging` key:

```yaml
logging:
  version: 1
  root: { level: INFO, handlers: [console] }
  handlers:
    console: { class: logging.StreamHandler, formatter: plain }
  formatters:
    plain: { format: "%(asctime)s %(levelname)-8s %(name)s: %(message)s" }
```

[^1]: Or the file passed with `--config`. Relative paths inside the file are resolved relative to the file itself, not the current working directory.
[^2]: Seriously, don't do that on the open internet.

Frequently Asked Questions
==========================

General
-------

### Is Widgets free?

Yes. Widgets is open source under the Apache 2.0 license. There is a hosted version, *Widgets Cloud*, which is a paid product, but everything in this repository is and will remain free.

### Who is behind it?
Widgets was started in 2019 by a small team at ACME and is now maintained by a group of volunteers and two full-time engineers. See the [governance page](governance.md).

Troubleshooting
---------------

### "Address already in use" when running `widgets serve`

Another process is listening on port 8050.  Either stop it or pick a different port:

    widgets serve --port 8051

On Linux you can find the culprit with `ss -ltnp | grep 8050`, on macOS with `lsof -iTCP:8050 -sTCP:LISTEN`.

### My dashboard is blank
> Check the browser console first. In nine out of ten cases a query failed and the error is logged there.
>
> If the console is clean, run the server with `--log-level debug` and look for lines starting with `query:`.
>> Tip: `widgets doctor` checks the most common misconfigurations automatically.

### The PDF export cuts off wide tables

This is a known limitation of the headless browser we use for printing. Workarounds, in order of preference:

1. switch the table to `layout: scroll`, which the exporter renders on multiple pages
1. reduce the font size with `print.font_scale: 0.8`
1. export as PNG instead

Roadmap
-------

Things we are working on for the next release:

- [x] Redis cache backend
- [x] Dark theme
- [ ] Row-level security for data sources
- [ ] Scheduled e-mail reports
  - [x] design doc
  - [ ] SMTP backend
  - [ ] templates
- [ ] ~~Excel export~~ (dropped, use CSV)

*Didn't find your question?* Ask in [Discussions](https://github.com/acme/widgets/discussions) or on the chat server; we're friendly.

# API reference #

The `widgets` Python API is __stable__ from version 3.0 on: anything documented on this page follows [semantic versioning](https://semver.org). Names starting with an underscore are _private_ and may change at any time.

## `widgets.Dashboard` ##

```python
class Dashboard(title: str, *, layout: Layout | None = None, theme: str = "default")
```

A container for widgets.

__Parameters__

* `title` -- shown above the dashboard.
* `layout` -- a `Layout` instance; defaults to a responsive 12-column grid.
* `theme` -- the name of a registered theme.

__Example__

```python
from widgets import Dashboard, Chart

dash = Dashboard("Sales")
dash.add(Chart.line(data="sales.csv", x="month", y="revenue"), row=0, col=0, width=8)
dash.serve()
```

### `Dashboard.add(widget, *, row, col, width=4, height=1)` ###
Adds a widget at the given grid position. Raises `LayoutError` if it overlaps another widget _and_ `allow_overlap` is false.

### `Dashboard.serve(host="127.0.0.1", port=8050, reload=False)` ###
Starts the development server. See [the CLI docs](cli.md#serve) for the equivalent command line flags.

## `widgets.Chart` ##

Factory functions: `Chart.line`, `Chart.bar`, `Chart.scatter`, `Chart.area`, `Chart.pie` (deprecated, use `Chart.donut`).

All factory functions accept the following keyword arguments:

Argument | Type | Description
:--|:--|:--
`data` | `str \| DataFrame \| DataSource` | Where the data comes from.
`x`, `y` | `str` | Column names.
`color` | `str \| None` | Column used for the colour encoding.
`title`| `str \| None` |
`tooltip` | `list[str]` | Columns shown on hover; defaults to `[x, y]`.

#### Deprecated: `Chart.pie` ####

> __Deprecated since 3.2:__ `Chart.pie` will be removed in 4.0. `Chart.donut(hole=0)` produces the same output.

## Exceptions ##

`WidgetsError`
: Base class for all exceptions raised by the library.

`LayoutError`
: Raised when widgets overlap or exceed the grid.

`DataSourceError`
: Raised when a data source cannot be reached. The original exception is available as `__cause__`.

# Architecture overview ![High-level architecture diagram showing the browser, the API gateway, the query service and the cache](images/architecture-overview.png "Architecture overview") Widgets consists of three processes that talk to each other over HTTP and Redis: 1. **The web server** serves the single-page application and the REST API. 2. **The query service** executes data source queries in a sandbox and streams results back. It is horizontally scalable; we run between 4 and 40 replicas depending on load. 3. **Redis** is used as a cache and as a message broker for long-running queries. ## Request lifecycle A request for a dashboard goes through the following steps (see the diagram above). The interesting part is step 4, where the query service decides whether a cached result is fresh enough; the rules for that are documented in detail at https://widgets.example.com/docs/internals/caching/freshness-rules-and-how-they-interact-with-row-level-security#freshness-rules and are summarised below. * The browser requests `/api/dashboards/{id}`. * The web server checks the session and loads the dashboard definition from Postgres. * For each widget, the web server asks the query service for data. * The query service computes a cache key from the query and its parameters. * On a hit, the cached result is returned immediately. * On a miss the query runs, with a timeout of `query.timeout` seconds (default 30). * Results are streamed back to the browser as [newline-delimited JSON](https://github.com/ndjson/ndjson-spec). ## Deployment We ship a [Helm chart](https://github.com/acme/widgets/tree/main/deploy/helm/widgets) and a [docker-compose file](https://github.com/acme/widgets/blob/main/deploy/compose/docker-compose.yml?plain=1#L1-L80). For a sense of scale, our largest known installation (around 2,000 dashboards and 15,000 daily users) runs on three nodes; see the case study at .
ComponentCPUMemory
web0.5512 MiB
query22 GiB
--- Questions? Mail or open a discussion.

---
title:    "What we learned migrating 400 services to OpenTelemetry"
date: 2026-03-14T09:30:00+01:00
draft: false
authors: [ "jdoe", 'msmith' ]
tags:
  - observability
  - opentelemetry
  -   migration
summary: >
  A year-long migration, three false starts, and one very large Grafana bill.
canonical_url: https://engineering.example.com/blog/2026/03/opentelemetry-migration/
---

When we started the migration in January 2025 we had three different tracing libraries, two metrics
pipelines and a logging setup that only one person fully understood. Fourteen months later
every service emits OpenTelemetry, the old collectors are switched off, and our observability bill is
down by roughly a third. This post is about the parts that went well, the parts that did not,
and the things we would do differently if we started again tomorrow.

## Why bother?

The short answer is vendor lock-in. The longer answer is that each of our three tracing libraries had its own idea of what a "service name" was, which made cross-team traces nearly useless: a request that went from the storefront through the checkout service into the payment gateway would show up as three disconnected traces in two different tools.

## Phase 1: the collector

We rolled out the OpenTelemetry Collector as a DaemonSet first, before touching a single
line of application code.     That gave us a single place to
receive, transform and export telemetry, and let us dual-write to the old and new backends
for a few months.

> The best migration is one where nobody notices the cut-over. We got close, but not quite: for about
> forty minutes on 2 June, every trace from the EU region was dropped because of a misconfigured
> memory limiter.

## Phase 2: libraries

This was the long part. Some numbers:

* 412 services in total
   * 290 Java (Spring Boot), most of which just needed the Java agent
   * 85 Go, which needed actual code changes
   * 37 Python, Node and "other"
* 3 services we decided to retire instead of migrating

The Go services were the hardest. Unlike Java, there is no agent that magically instruments everything, so every HTTP handler, every database call and every Kafka consumer had to be wrapped by hand -- or, more often, by a codemod we wrote for the purpose and then spent weeks debugging. If you are about to do the same, look at [the contrib instrumentation packages](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go-contrib/tree/main/instrumentation) first; many of the wrappers we wrote turned out to exist already.

## What we'd do differently


1. Agree on semantic conventions *before* writing code.
2. Budget for the collector's memory. Seriously.
3. Turn on tail sampling earlier -- it cut our span volume by 80%.

---

*Thanks to everyone on the platform team, and to the 60+ service owners who reviewed our pull requests. Special thanks to Dr. Ana Pereira for the sampling math.*

Upgrading to Widgets 3.0
========================

Widgets 3.0 is the first major release in three years. Most projects will be able to upgrade by changing a handful of lines, but a few long-deprecated APIs are finally gone.  This guide lists everything you need to check, roughly ordered from "affects everyone" to "affects almost nobody".

**TL;DR**

1. Upgrade to the latest 2.x release first and fix all deprecation warnings.
2. Run `widgets migrate --check` -- it reports everything that needs to change.
3. Run `widgets migrate --write` to apply the automatic fixes, then review the diff.

Python version
--------------
Python 3.10 is now the minimum supported version.

Configuration file
------------------

The configuration file is now called `widgets.yml` (previously `widgets.yaml` *or* `.widgetsrc`).  Both old names still work in 3.0 but emit a warning; they will stop working in 3.1.

Several keys were renamed:

| 2.x | 3.0 |
|-----|-----|
| `port` | `server.port` |
| `host` | `server.host` |
| `cache_type` | `cache.backend` |
| `redis_url` | `cache.url` |
| `debug` | *removed* — use `--log-level debug` |

Before:

```yaml
port: 8080
cache_type: redis
redis_url: "redis://localhost:6379/0"
debug: true
```

After:

```yaml
server:
  port: 8080
cache:
  backend: redis
  url: redis://localhost:6379/0
```

Python API
----------

### `Dashboard.render()` returns a `RenderResult`

In 2.x, `render()` returned an HTML string. It now returns a `RenderResult` object with `.html`, `.assets` and `.warnings` attributes. If you only need the HTML:

```diff
-html = dash.render()
+html = dash.render().html
```

### Removed: `widgets.contrib`

Everything in `widgets.contrib` was either promoted to the main package or moved to a separate distribution:

* `widgets.contrib.maps` → `widgets-maps` on PyPI
* `widgets.contrib.auth.ldap` → `widgets-ldap`
* `widgets.contrib.charts.sankey` → now `widgets.Chart.sankey`

### Deprecated in 3.0, removed in 4.0
- `Chart.pie` (use `Chart.donut`)
- the `theme="classic"` alias

Getting help
------------

If something in this guide is wrong or missing, please [open an issue](https://github.com/acme/widgets/issues/new?template=upgrade.yml&labels=upgrade-3.0&title=%5BUpgrade+3.0%5D+) -- we'd rather fix the guide than have you figure it out alone.

# Architecture overview ![High-level architecture diagram showing the browser, the API gateway, the query service and the cache](images/architecture-overview.png "Architecture overview") Widgets consists of three processes that talk to each other over HTTP and Redis: 1. **The web server** serves the single-page application and the REST API. 2. **The query service** executes data source queries in a sandbox and streams results back. It is horizontally scalable; we run between 4 and 40 replicas depending on load. 3. **Redis** is used as a cache and as a message broker for long-running queries. ## Request lifecycle A request for a dashboard goes through the following steps (see the diagram above). The interesting part is step 4, where the query service decides whether a cached result is fresh enough; the rules for that are documented in detail at https://widgets.example.com/docs/internals/caching/freshness-rules-and-how-they-interact-with-row-level-security#freshness-rules and are summarised below. * The browser requests `/api/dashboards/{id}`. * The web server checks the session and loads the dashboard definition from Postgres. * For each widget, the web server asks the query service for data. * The query service computes a cache key from the query and its parameters. * On a hit, the cached result is returned immediately. * On a miss the query runs, with a timeout of `query.timeout` seconds (default 30). * Results are streamed back to the browser as [newline-delimited JSON](https://github.com/ndjson/ndjson-spec). ## Deployment We ship a [Helm chart](https://github.com/acme/widgets/tree/main/deploy/helm/widgets) and a [docker-compose file](https://github.com/acme/widgets/blob/main/deploy/compose/docker-compose.yml?plain=1#L1-L80). For a sense of scale, our largest known installation (around 2,000 dashboards and 15,000 daily users) runs on three nodes; see the case study at .

title:    "What we learned migrating 400 services to OpenTelemetry"
date: 2026-03-14T09:30:00+01:00
draft: false
authors: [ "jdoe", 'msmith' ]
tags:
  - observability
  - opentelemetry
  -   migration
summary: >
  A year-long migration, three false starts, and one very large Grafana bill.
canonical_url: https://engineering.example.com/blog/2026/03/opentelemetry-migration/
---

When we started the migration in January 2025 we had three different tracing libraries, two metrics
pipelines and a logging setup that only one person fully understood. Fourteen months later
every service emits OpenTelemetry, the old collectors are switched off, and our observability bill is
down by roughly a third. This post is about the parts that went well, the parts that did not,
and the things we would do differently if we started again tomorrow.

## Why bother?

The short answer is vendor lock-in. The longer answer is that each of our three tracing libraries had its own idea of what a "service name" was, which made cross-team traces nearly useless: a request that went from the storefront through the checkout service into the payment gateway would show up as three disconnected traces in two different tools.

## Phase 1: the collector

We rolled out the OpenTelemetry Collector as a DaemonSet first, before touching a single
line of application code.     That gave us a single place to
receive, transform and export telemetry, and let us dual-write to the old and new backends
for a few months.

> The best migration is one where nobody notices the cut-over. We got close, but not quite: for about
> forty minutes on 2 June, every trace from the EU region was dropped because of a misconfigured
> memory limiter.

## Phase 2: libraries

This was the long part. Some numbers:

* 412 services in total
   * 290 Java (Spring Boot), most of which just needed the Java agent
   * 85 Go, which needed actual code changes
   * 37 Python, Node and "other"
* 3 services we decided to retire instead of migrating

The Go services were the hardest. Unlike Java, there is no agent that magically instruments everything, so every HTTP handler, every database call and every Kafka consumer had to be wrapped by hand -- or, more often, by a codemod we wrote for the purpose and then spent weeks debugging. If you are about to do the same, look at [the contrib instrumentation packages](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go-contrib/tree/main/instrumentation) first; many of the wrappers we wrote turned out to exist already.

## What we'd do differently


1. Agree on semantic conventions *before* writing code.
2. Budget for the collector's memory. Seriously.
3. Turn on tail sampling earlier -- it cut our span volume by 80%.

---

*Thanks to everyone on the platform team, and to the 60+ service owners who reviewed our pull requests. Special thanks to Dr. Ana Pereira for the sampling math.*

# Deploying to production

> [!NOTE]
> This guide assumes you have already completed the [staging setup](staging.md).

> [!TIP]
> Use `widgets doctor --production` to catch the most common misconfigurations before you deploy.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Starting with 3.2, the server refuses to start in production mode without `auth` configured.

## Checklist

1. Put a reverse proxy (nginx, Caddy, Traefik...) in front of the server and terminate TLS there.
2. Set `server.workers` to the number of CPU cores, or `2 * cores + 1` if most of your queries are I/O bound.
3. Use the `redis` cache backend so all workers share one cache.
4. Configure log shipping.

> [!WARNING]
> Do **not** expose the Redis instance to the internet. Widgets stores
> cached query results in it, which may include personal data.

> [!CAUTION]
> Running `widgets cache clear --all` in production will cause a thundering herd of queries against your databases. Prefer clearing individual data sources.

## Reverse proxy example

<details>
<summary>nginx</summary>

```nginx
server {
    listen 443 ssl http2;
    server_name dashboards.example.com;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8050;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    }
}
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>Caddy</summary>

```
dashboards.example.com {
    reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8050
}
```
</details>

---
title: "Build a command-line tool in Python: from script to package"
author: Kim Example
date: 2026-08-02
tags: [python, cli, packaging, tutorial]
toc: true
---

Build a command-line tool in Python
===================================

*From a throwaway script to a package you can `pip install`, in about an hour.*

<!-- TODO(kim): add a screenshot of the final tool once the colours are settled -->

Most useful tools start life as a script in someone's home directory. That's fine! But at some point other
people want to use it, and then you need a proper command line interface, help text, tests, and a way to
install it that doesn't involve "copy this file somewhere on your PATH and hope". This tutorial walks
through that transition step by step, using a small but real example: a tool that finds duplicate files.

Contents
--------

1. [The starting point](#the-starting-point)
2. [Adding a CLI with argparse](#adding-a-cli-with-argparse)
3. [Packaging](#packaging)
4. [Testing](#testing)
5. [Publishing](#publishing)

The starting point
------------------

Here is the script we start from. It walks a directory tree, hashes every file, and prints groups of files with identical hashes:

~~~python
import hashlib, os, sys
from collections import defaultdict

hashes = defaultdict(list)
for root, dirs, files in os.walk(sys.argv[1]):
    for name in files:
        path = os.path.join(root, name)
        with open(path, "rb") as f:
            hashes[hashlib.sha256(f.read()).hexdigest()].append(path)

for h, paths in hashes.items():
    if len(paths) > 1:
        print(h[:12], *paths, sep="\n  ")
~~~

It works, but it has problems:

* it reads every file completely into memory (try it on a directory with a 20 GB video file...)
* there is no `--help`
* errors (permission denied, broken symlinks) crash the whole thing
* it hashes *every* file, even though files of different sizes can't possibly be duplicates

Let's fix these one at a time.

Adding a CLI with argparse
--------------------------

The standard library's `argparse` is perfectly adequate for a tool of this size.  Third-party libraries like [Click](https://click.palletsprojects.com/) or [Typer](https://typer.tiangolo.com/) are nicer for big CLIs with many sub-commands, but they are an extra dependency, and for a single command `argparse` is hard to beat.

```python
import argparse

def parse_args(argv=None):
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="dupfind", description="Find duplicate files.")
    p.add_argument("paths", nargs="+", help="directories to scan")
    p.add_argument("--min-size", type=int, default=1, metavar="BYTES",
                   help="ignore files smaller than this (default: %(default)s)")
    p.add_argument("--json", action="store_true", help="print results as JSON")
    return p.parse_args(argv)
```

> **Tip:** always accept an `argv` parameter in `parse_args`. It makes the function trivial to test,
> because you can pass a list of strings instead of patching `sys.argv`.

### Hashing in chunks

Reading in chunks keeps memory use constant:

    def file_hash(path, chunk_size=1 << 20):
        h = hashlib.sha256()
        with open(path, "rb") as f:
            while chunk := f.read(chunk_size):
                h.update(chunk)
        return h.hexdigest()

### Grouping by size first ###

Two files can only be identical if they have the same size, and `os.stat` is
*much* cheaper than reading the file.  So we group by size first, and only hash files
whose size is shared with at least one other file.  On my laptop's home
directory (412,000 files) this reduces the number of files hashed from 412,000 to about
31,000 and the run time from 4 min 10 s to 22 s.

Packaging
---------

Create a `pyproject.toml` next to your code:

```toml
[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

[project]
name = "dupfind"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Find duplicate files, fast."

# 7. Use PostgreSQL for the metadata store

Date: 2026-01-22

## Status

Accepted

Supersedes [3. Use SQLite for the metadata store](0003-use-sqlite-for-metadata.md)

## Context

The metadata store holds dashboard definitions, users, permissions and audit events. Since ADR 3 we have stored all of it in a single SQLite file next to the server process. That was fine for the single-node deployments we had in mind at the time, but:

* customers increasingly run several server replicas behind a load balancer, which SQLite cannot support without a shared filesystem (and SQLite over NFS is a known source of corruption);
* the audit log grows by ~2 GB/month on our largest installation and SQLite's `VACUUM` locks the database for minutes;
* we want to use row-level security for the multi-tenant cloud offering.

We considered the following options:

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| Keep SQLite, add Litestream | no new dependency; easy backups | still single-writer; no RLS |
| PostgreSQL | mature, RLS, logical replication, everyone knows it | one more service to run |
| MySQL 8 | widely available in managed form | weaker JSON support, no RLS |
| CockroachDB | horizontally scalable | licence change in 2024, operational complexity |

## Decision

We will use **PostgreSQL 15 or newer** as the only supported metadata store from Widgets 3.0 on. SQLite remains supported for local development and tests only.

## Consequences

+ Deployments need a PostgreSQL instance. The Helm chart gets an optional Bitnami PostgreSQL dependency, and the docker-compose file gets a `db` service.
+ We can drop the hand-written locking code around SQLite writes (~1,200 lines).
+ Migrations move from our home-grown runner to Alembic.

- Small self-hosted installations become slightly harder to run. We will publish a "single container" image with an embedded PostgreSQL for this case.
- Our CI matrix grows: every supported PostgreSQL major version has to be tested.

title: "Build a command-line tool in Python: from script to package"
author: Kim Example
date: 2026-08-02
tags: [python, cli, packaging, tutorial]
toc: true
---

Build a command-line tool in Python
===================================

*From a throwaway script to a package you can `pip install`, in about an hour.*

<!-- TODO(kim): add a screenshot of the final tool once the colours are settled -->

Most useful tools start life as a script in someone's home directory. That's fine! But at some point other
people want to use it, and then you need a proper command line interface, help text, tests, and a way to
install it that doesn't involve "copy this file somewhere on your PATH and hope". This tutorial walks
through that transition step by step, using a small but real example: a tool that finds duplicate files.

Contents
--------

1. [The starting point](#the-starting-point)
2. [Adding a CLI with argparse](#adding-a-cli-with-argparse)
3. [Packaging](#packaging)
4. [Testing](#testing)
5. [Publishing](#publishing)

The starting point
------------------

Here is the script we start from. It walks a directory tree, hashes every file, and prints groups of files with identical hashes:

~~~python
import hashlib, os, sys
from collections import defaultdict

hashes = defaultdict(list)
for root, dirs, files in os.walk(sys.argv[1]):
    for name in files:
        path = os.path.join(root, name)
        with open(path, "rb") as f:
            hashes[hashlib.sha256(f.read()).hexdigest()].append(path)

for h, paths in hashes.items():
    if len(paths) > 1:
        print(h[:12], *paths, sep="\n  ")
~~~

It works, but it has problems:

* it reads every file completely into memory (try it on a directory with a 20 GB video file...)
* there is no `--help`
* errors (permission denied, broken symlinks) crash the whole thing
* it hashes *every* file, even though files of different sizes can't possibly be duplicates

Let's fix these one at a time.

Adding a CLI with argparse
--------------------------

The standard library's `argparse` is perfectly adequate for a tool of this size.  Third-party libraries like [Click](https://click.palletsprojects.com/) or [Typer](https://typer.tiangolo.com/) are nicer for big CLIs with many sub-commands, but they are an extra dependency, and for a single command `argparse` is hard to beat.

```python
import argparse

def parse_args(argv=None):
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="dupfind", description="Find duplicate files.")
    p.add_argument("paths", nargs="+", help="directories to scan")
    p.add_argument("--min-size", type=int, default=1, metavar="BYTES",
                   help="ignore files smaller than this (default: %(default)s)")
    p.add_argument("--json", action="store_true", help="print results as JSON")
    return p.parse_args(argv)
```

> **Tip:** always accept an `argv` parameter in `parse_args`. It makes the function trivial to test,
> because you can pass a list of strings instead of patching `sys.argv`.

### Hashing in chunks

Reading in chunks keeps memory use constant:

    def file_hash(path, chunk_size=1 << 20):
        h = hashlib.sha256()
        with open(path, "rb") as f:
            while chunk := f.read(chunk_size):
                h.update(chunk)
        return h.hexdigest()

### Grouping by size first ###

Two files can only be identical if they have the same size, and `os.stat` is
*much* cheaper than reading the file.  So we group by size first, and only hash files
whose size is shared with at least one other file.  On my laptop's home
directory (412,000 files) this reduces the number of files hashed from 412,000 to about
31,000 and the run time from 4 min 10 s to 22 s.

Packaging
---------

Create a `pyproject.toml` next to your code:

```toml
[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

[project]
name = "dupfind"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Find duplicate files, fast."
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.10"
license = "MIT"
authors = [{ name = "Kim Example", email = "kim@example.com" }]

[project.scripts]
dupfind = "dupfind.cli:main"
```

The `[project.scripts]` table is the important part: it tells the installer to create a `dupfind` executable that calls `main()` in `dupfind/cli.py`.

The project layout should look like this:

```
dupfind/
├── pyproject.toml
├── README.md
├── src/
│   └── dupfind/
│       ├── __init__.py
│       └── cli.py
└── tests/
    └── test_cli.py
```

Install it in editable mode while you work on it:

```console
$ python -m pip install -e .
$ dupfind --help
usage: dupfind [-h] [--min-size BYTES] [--json] paths [paths ...]
```

Testing
-------

Use `pytest` and its `tmp_path` fixture to create throwaway directory trees:

```python
def test_finds_duplicates(tmp_path, capsys):
    (tmp_path / "a.txt").write_text("hello")
    (tmp_path / "b.txt").write_text("hello")
    (tmp_path / "c.txt").write_text("world")

    assert main([str(tmp_path), "--json"]) == 0
    out = json.loads(capsys.readouterr().out)
    assert len(out) == 1
    assert sorted(Path(p).name for p in out[0]["paths"]) == ["a.txt", "b.txt"]
```

Things worth testing, roughly in order of importance:

1) the happy path (duplicates are found)
2) no false positives (same size, different content)
3) unreadable files are skipped with a warning, not a crash
4) `--min-size` is respected

| Test | What it catches | Runtime |
|---|---|--:|
| `test_finds_duplicates` | basic regressions | 4 ms |
| `test_same_size_different_content` | hashing shortcuts gone wrong | 3 ms |
| `test_permission_denied` | crashes on unreadable files (skipped on Windows) | 6 ms |
| `test_min_size` | option parsing | 2 ms |

Publishing
----------

Build the distribution files and upload them with [twine](https://twine.readthedocs.io/):

```bash
python -m pip install build twine
python -m build
python -m twine upload dist/*
```

Better yet, let GitHub Actions do it with [trusted publishing][trusted-publishing], so you never have to handle an API token at all. The workflow is only a few lines long, and once it is set up, releasing is just a matter of pushing a tag.

***

Wrapping up
-----------

That's it -- you now have a tool that is installable, testable, and documented.  Some ideas for next steps:

- add a `--delete` flag (with a *very* clear confirmation prompt)
- parallelise hashing with `concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor`
    - note that hashing is mostly I/O-bound, so threads are fine here
    - on spinning disks, more than 2-4 threads usually makes things *slower*
- support `.dupfindignore` files using the same syntax as `.gitignore`
- add shell completion with [argcomplete](https://github.com/kislyuk/argcomplete)

If you build something with this, I'd love to hear about it: <kim@example.com>.\
Happy hacking!

title:  "Palmer penguins: bill dimensions by species"
subtitle: An exploratory analysis
author:

        department: Department of Ecology

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
```

## Introduction {#sec-intro}

The Palmer Archipelago penguins dataset [@horst2020; @gorman2014] contains size measurements for three penguin species observed on three islands in the Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica. It has become a popular alternative to the iris dataset for teaching, partly because it contains missing values and a mix of numeric and categorical variables, which makes it a more realistic first dataset than iris ever was.

In this document we look at the relationship between bill length and bill depth (@fig-bill-scatter) and summarise the measurements by species (@tbl-summary). See @sec-methods for details on how missing values were handled.

::: {.callout-note}
The data were collected by Dr. Kristen Gorman between 2007 and 2009 as part of the Palmer Station Long Term Ecological Research program.
:::

## Methods {#sec-methods}

Rows with missing bill measurements were dropped (n = `r sum(is.na(penguins$bill_length_mm))`).  We fitted a simple linear model

$$
\text{depth}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \, \text{length}_i + \beta_2 \, \text{species}_i + \varepsilon_i
$$ {#eq-model}

where $\varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$.  Ignoring species (i.e. dropping $\beta_2$) produces a *negative* slope -- a textbook example of Simpson's paradox.

## Results

```{r}
#| label: fig-bill-scatter
#| fig-cap: "Bill length vs. bill depth. Each point is one penguin; lines are per-species linear fits."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height:   5
#| fig-alt: "Scatterplot with three clusters of points, one per species, each with a positive linear trend."
penguins |>
  drop_na(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm) |>
  ggplot(aes(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)", colour = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-summary
#| tbl-cap: Mean bill measurements by species
#| echo: true
penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(across(c(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm), \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)), n = n()) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## Caveat about the model

The model in @eq-model assumes the same slope for all species. An interaction term would be more appropriate if we were interested in species-specific slopes; we are not, for now.
:::

## Discussion

Within each species, longer bills are deeper.  Across species the relationship reverses, because Gentoo penguins have long but shallow bills.[^1]

[^1]: For more on this see @fig-bill-scatter and the original paper by @gorman2014.

## References {.unnumbered}

::: {#refs}
:::

---
title: "Bayesian A/B testing without the tears"
description: "A gentle, mostly code-free introduction to Beta-Binomial A/B tests, with a small simulation at the end."
author: Robin Example
date: "2026-06-20"
categories: [statistics, bayesian,  "a/b testing" ]
image: thumbnail.png
draft: false
bibliography: refs.bib
csl: ../../chicago-author-date.csl
citation: true
---

Most A/B tests I see in industry are analysed with a two-proportion z-test, which is fine, but the
results are routinely misinterpreted: "there is a 95% chance that B is better than A" is *not* what a
p-value of 0.05 means [@greenland2016].   A Bayesian analysis answers that question directly, and for
conversion rates the maths is simple enough to do in your head (almost).

## The Beta-Binomial model

If a variant has $n$ visitors and $k$ conversions, and our prior belief about its conversion rate $p$ is $\text{Beta}(\alpha, \beta)$, then the posterior is

$$
p \mid k, n \sim \text{Beta}(\alpha + k,\; \beta + n - k).
$$

That's it -- no MCMC, no Stan, no tears. See @gelman2013 [ch. 2] for the derivation.

## A simulation

```{r}
#| label: sim
#| code-fold: show
set.seed(42)
a <- rbeta(1e5, 1 + 120, 1 + 2400 - 120)
b <- rbeta(1e5, 1 + 145, 1 + 2380 - 145)
mean(b > a)
```

So, given the data and a flat prior, there is roughly a `r round(100 * mean(b > a))`% probability that B converts better than A.

::: {.callout-important}
## Don't peek (too much)
Bayesian methods are *less* sensitive to optional stopping than frequentist ones, but they are not immune. If you check the results every hour and stop as soon as $P(B > A) > 0.95$, you will still fool yourself more often than you expect [@rouder2014].
:::

## Further reading

- @kruschke2014 is the friendliest book-length introduction.
- For a more industry-focused take, the [Evan Miller blog post on Bayesian A/B testing](https://www.evanmiller.org/bayesian-ab-testing.html) is a classic.
