---
title: "Seasonal variation in urban bird song frequency"
author:
  - name: A. Researcher
    corresponding: true
    email: a.researcher@example.edu
    affiliations: [ { name: "Example University", city: Leeds, country: UK } ]
  - name: B. Collaborator
    affiliations:
      - name: Institute of Acoustics
abstract: |
  Urban birds sing at higher minimum frequencies than their rural conspecifics, a pattern usually attributed to masking by low-frequency traffic noise. We recorded 1,240 songs from 86 great tits (*Parus major*) across one year and show that the urban--rural difference is largest in spring, when traffic noise is lowest.
keywords: [bioacoustics, urban ecology, noise]
format:
  html: default
  pdf:
    keep-tex: true
    include-in-header:
      text: |
        \usepackage{siunitx}
number-sections: true
crossref:
  fig-prefix: Figure
  eq-prefix: Eq.
bibliography: references.bib
---

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Anthropogenic noise is now recognised as a pervasive pollutant [@slabbekoorn2003; @brumm2004], and its effects on acoustic communication have been documented across taxa, from insects to whales.  In birds, the best studied response is an upward shift of the minimum song frequency, which reduces masking by low-frequency noise but may carry costs in mate attraction [@halfwerk2011].

# Methods {#sec-methods}

## Recordings

Songs were recorded at 12 sites (6 urban, 6 rural; @tbl-sites) between January and December 2024 using a Sennheiser ME67 shotgun microphone and a Zoom F3 recorder (48 kHz, 24 bit).

| Site | Habitat | Mean noise level (dB(A)) | Songs |
|------|---------|-------------------------:|------:|
| Leeds city centre | urban | 62.1 | 134 |
| Roundhay Park | urban | 51.4 | 118 |
| Otley Chevin | rural | 38.9 | 97 |

: Recording sites (subset; full table in the supplement). {#tbl-sites}

## Statistical analysis

We modelled minimum song frequency $f_{\min}$ with a linear mixed model:

$$
f_{\min, ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{urban}_j + \beta_2 \text{season}_{ij} + \beta_3 (\text{urban} \times \text{season})_{ij} + u_j + \epsilon_{ij}
$$ {#eq-lmm}

where $u_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_u^2)$ is a random intercept for individual $j$. Models were fitted with **lme4** [@bates2015] in R 4.4.

# Results {#sec-results}

Urban birds sang with a higher minimum frequency than rural birds in all seasons (@fig-season; $\beta_1 = 312$ Hz, 95% CI 254--370). The interaction term in @eq-lmm was significant (p < 0.001).

::: {#fig-season layout-ncol=2}

![Spring](figures/spring.png){#fig-spring}

![Winter](figures/winter.png){#fig-winter}

Minimum song frequency by habitat in spring (a) and winter (b). Boxes show the interquartile range; whiskers extend to 1.5 × IQR.
:::

# Discussion

Contrary to the masking hypothesis, the urban--rural difference was *largest* in spring (@fig-spring), when traffic noise was lowest, e.g. during the Easter school holidays. One explanation, suggested by Dr. Halfwerk (pers. comm.), is that spring is when song matters most for mate attraction, so selection for being heard is strongest then.

# References {.unnumbered}

::: {#refs}
:::

---
title: Getting started with targets
author: "R Users Group"
format:
  html:
    code-copy: true
    callout-appearance: simple
    callout-icon: false
filters:
  - include-code-files

{{< include _common.qmd >}}

[targets](https://docs.ropensci.org/targets/) is a pipeline tool for R.  It skips steps that are already up to date, runs independent steps in parallel, and makes it easy to see which parts of an analysis depend on which data.

::: callout-note
This tutorial assumes **targets** 1.7 or later. Check with `packageVersion("targets")`.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Use a project"}
Create an RStudio project (or a Positron folder) for the tutorial so that relative paths work.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Expand: what if I already have a `_targets.R`?
Move it out of the way first -- `tar_script()` will refuse to overwrite it, and you probably don't want to lose your existing pipeline.
:::

## Step 1: write the pipeline

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| filename: "_targets.R"
library(targets)
tar_option_set(packages = c("readr", "dplyr", "ggplot2"))

list(
  tar_target(file, "data/raw.csv", format = "file"),
  tar_target(raw, read_csv(file, col_types = cols())),
  tar_target(clean, raw |> filter(!is.na(value)) |> mutate(value = as.numeric(value))),
  tar_target(plot, ggplot(clean, aes(date, value)) + geom_line())
)
```

## Step 2: run it

::: {.panel-tabset group="ide"}
### RStudio
Click **Build > Run targets** or press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>B</kbd>.

### Console
```{r}
#| eval: false
targets::tar_make()
```
:::

::: {.callout-important}
`tar_make()` runs the pipeline in a **fresh R session**. Objects in your global environment are not visible to it -- everything a target needs must be loaded by `_targets.R`.
:::

## Step 3: inspect

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
tar_visnetwork()
tar_read(plot)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistake
Forgetting `format = "file"` for input files means targets will not notice when the *contents* of the file change.
:::

execute:
  echo: true

# Dates and times {#sec-dates}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
library(lubridate)
library(dplyr)
```

Dates look simple until you have to compute with them. How many days are there between 1 February and 1 March? It depends on the year. What time is it in Sydney when it's 9 am in London? It depends on the day, because the two cities switch to daylight saving time in opposite halves of the year. This chapter shows how to handle these questions in R without losing your mind; we'll build on it in @sec-time-series and @sec-joins-by-time.

## Parsing dates

Most dates arrive as strings[^iso]. The **lubridate** functions `ymd()`, `dmy()`, `mdy()` and friends are named after the order of the components, and they're forgiving about separators:

```{r}
ymd("2026-03-14")
dmy("14/03/2026")
mdy("March 14th, 2026")
```

[^iso]: If you get to choose the format, choose ISO 8601 (`YYYY-MM-DD`). It sorts correctly as text, and nobody can misread `2026-03-04` as April 3rd.

If the string also contains a time, add the time components to the function name, e.g. `ymd_hms()`.  The result is a date-time (class `POSIXct`), which by default is in UTC -- [a common source of confusion]{.mark} when your data was recorded in local time.

### Time zones

```{r}
#| label: tz-example
x <- ymd_hms("2026-03-29 00:30:00", tz = "Europe/London")
x + hours(1)
with_tz(x, "Australia/Sydney")
```

Notice anything odd? 29 March 2026 is the day the UK switches to summer time, so one hour after 00:30 GMT is 02:30 BST.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
`OlsonNames()` lists every time zone name R knows about. There are more than 590 of them.
:::

## Arithmetic

lubridate distinguishes three kinds of time spans:

* **durations** are an exact number of seconds (`ddays(1)` is always 86,400 s),
* **periods** are human units like "one month", whose length in seconds depends on when they start,
* **intervals** have a fixed start and end.

| You want to... | Use |
|:--|:--|
| add "one month" to a billing date | a period: `%m+% months(1)` |
| measure how long a job ran | a duration |
| check whether a timestamp falls inside a maintenance window | an interval and `%within%` |

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1.  What does `ymd("2026-02-30")` return, and why?
2.  Use `floor_date()` to count the number of rows per ISO week in the `flights` data.
3.  A meeting is scheduled for 09:00 in New York on the 4th of every month in 2027. Write code that lists the corresponding local times in Berlin.  Which months are unusual, and why?

    ```{r}
    #| eval: false
    #| code-fold: true
    meetings <- ymd_hm("2027-01-04 09:00", tz = "America/New_York") + months(0:11)
    with_tz(meetings, "Europe/Berlin")
    ```

{{< pagebreak >}}

## Summary

Dates and times are hard because the rules for them were made by people, not by mathematicians.^[And by politicians, who change the daylight saving rules more often than you'd think.] lubridate hides most of the complexity, but it can't hide all of it -- always check the time zone of your data.

subtitle: An exploratory analysis
author:

---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
```

## Introduction {#sec-intro}

The Palmer Archipelago penguins dataset [@horst2020; @gorman2014] contains size measurements for three penguin species observed on three islands in the Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica. It has become a popular alternative to the iris dataset for teaching, partly because it contains missing values and a mix of numeric and categorical variables, which makes it a more realistic first dataset than iris ever was.

In this document we look at the relationship between bill length and bill depth (@fig-bill-scatter) and summarise the measurements by species (@tbl-summary). See @sec-methods for details on how missing values were handled.

::: {.callout-note}
The data were collected by Dr. Kristen Gorman between 2007 and 2009 as part of the Palmer Station Long Term Ecological Research program.
:::

## Methods {#sec-methods}

Rows with missing bill measurements were dropped (n = `r sum(is.na(penguins$bill_length_mm))`).  We fitted a simple linear model

$$
\text{depth}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \, \text{length}_i + \beta_2 \, \text{species}_i + \varepsilon_i
$$ {#eq-model}

where $\varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$.  Ignoring species (i.e. dropping $\beta_2$) produces a *negative* slope -- a textbook example of Simpson's paradox.

## Results

```{r}
#| label: fig-bill-scatter
#| fig-cap: "Bill length vs. bill depth. Each point is one penguin; lines are per-species linear fits."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height:   5
#| fig-alt: "Scatterplot with three clusters of points, one per species, each with a positive linear trend."
penguins |>
  drop_na(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm) |>
  ggplot(aes(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)", colour = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-summary
#| tbl-cap: Mean bill measurements by species
#| echo: true
penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(across(c(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm), \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)), n = n()) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## Caveat about the model

The model in @eq-model assumes the same slope for all species. An interaction term would be more appropriate if we were interested in species-specific slopes; we are not, for now.
:::

## Discussion

Within each species, longer bills are deeper.  Across species the relationship reverses, because Gentoo penguins have long but shallow bills.[^1]

[^1]: For more on this see @fig-bill-scatter and the original paper by @gorman2014.

## References {.unnumbered}

::: {#refs}
:::

|------|---------|-------------------------:|------:|
| Leeds city centre | urban | 62.1 | 134 |
| Roundhay Park | urban | 51.4 | 118 |
| Otley Chevin | rural | 38.9 | 97 |

: Recording sites (subset; full table in the supplement). {#tbl-sites}

## Statistical analysis

We modelled minimum song frequency $f_{\min}$ with a linear mixed model:

$$
f_{\min, ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{urban}_j + \beta_2 \text{season}_{ij} + \beta_3 (\text{urban} \times \text{season})_{ij} + u_j + \epsilon_{ij}
$$ {#eq-lmm}

where $u_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_u^2)$ is a random intercept for individual $j$. Models were fitted with **lme4** [@bates2015] in R 4.4.

# Results {#sec-results}

Urban birds sang with a higher minimum frequency than rural birds in all seasons (@fig-season; $\beta_1 = 312$ Hz, 95% CI 254--370). The interaction term in @eq-lmm was significant (p < 0.001).

::: {#fig-season layout-ncol=2}

![Spring](figures/spring.png){#fig-spring}

![Winter](figures/winter.png){#fig-winter}

Minimum song frequency by habitat in spring (a) and winter (b). Boxes show the interquartile range; whiskers extend to 1.5 × IQR.
:::

# Discussion

Contrary to the masking hypothesis, the urban--rural difference was *largest* in spring (@fig-spring), when traffic noise was lowest, e.g. during the Easter school holidays. One explanation, suggested by Dr. Halfwerk (pers. comm.), is that spring is when song matters most for mate attraction, so selection for being heard is strongest then.

[targets](https://docs.ropensci.org/targets/) is a pipeline tool for R.  It skips steps that are already up to date, runs independent steps in parallel, and makes it easy to see which parts of an analysis depend on which data.

::: callout-note
This tutorial assumes **targets** 1.7 or later. Check with `packageVersion("targets")`.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Use a project"}
Create an RStudio project (or a Positron folder) for the tutorial so that relative paths work.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Expand: what if I already have a `_targets.R`?
Move it out of the way first -- `tar_script()` will refuse to overwrite it, and you probably don't want to lose your existing pipeline.
:::

## Step 1: write the pipeline

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| filename: "_targets.R"
library(targets)
tar_option_set(packages = c("readr", "dplyr", "ggplot2"))

list(
  tar_target(file, "data/raw.csv", format = "file"),
  tar_target(raw, read_csv(file, col_types = cols())),
  tar_target(clean, raw |> filter(!is.na(value)) |> mutate(value = as.numeric(value))),
  tar_target(plot, ggplot(clean, aes(date, value)) + geom_line())
)
```

## Step 2: run it

::: {.panel-tabset group="ide"}
### RStudio
Click **Build > Run targets** or press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>B</kbd>.

### Console
```{r}
#| eval: false
targets::tar_make()
```
:::

::: {.callout-important}
`tar_make()` runs the pipeline in a **fresh R session**. Objects in your global environment are not visible to it -- everything a target needs must be loaded by `_targets.R`.
:::

## Step 3: inspect

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
tar_visnetwork()
tar_read(plot)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistake
Forgetting `format = "file"` for input files means targets will not notice when the *contents* of the file change.
:::

# Dates and times {#sec-dates}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
library(lubridate)
library(dplyr)
```

Dates look simple until you have to compute with them. How many days are there between 1 February and 1 March? It depends on the year. What time is it in Sydney when it's 9 am in London? It depends on the day, because the two cities switch to daylight saving time in opposite halves of the year. This chapter shows how to handle these questions in R without losing your mind; we'll build on it in @sec-time-series and @sec-joins-by-time.

## Parsing dates

Most dates arrive as strings[^iso]. The **lubridate** functions `ymd()`, `dmy()`, `mdy()` and friends are named after the order of the components, and they're forgiving about separators:

```{r}
ymd("2026-03-14")
dmy("14/03/2026")
mdy("March 14th, 2026")
```

[^iso]: If you get to choose the format, choose ISO 8601 (`YYYY-MM-DD`). It sorts correctly as text, and nobody can misread `2026-03-04` as April 3rd.

If the string also contains a time, add the time components to the function name, e.g. `ymd_hms()`.  The result is a date-time (class `POSIXct`), which by default is in UTC -- [a common source of confusion]{.mark} when your data was recorded in local time.

### Time zones

```{r}
#| label: tz-example
x <- ymd_hms("2026-03-29 00:30:00", tz = "Europe/London")
x + hours(1)
with_tz(x, "Australia/Sydney")
```

Notice anything odd? 29 March 2026 is the day the UK switches to summer time, so one hour after 00:30 GMT is 02:30 BST.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
`OlsonNames()` lists every time zone name R knows about. There are more than 590 of them.
:::

## Arithmetic

lubridate distinguishes three kinds of time spans:

* **durations** are an exact number of seconds (`ddays(1)` is always 86,400 s),
* **periods** are human units like "one month", whose length in seconds depends on when they start,
* **intervals** have a fixed start and end.

| You want to... | Use |
|:--|:--|
| add "one month" to a billing date | a period: `%m+% months(1)` |
| measure how long a job ran | a duration |
| check whether a timestamp falls inside a maintenance window | an interval and `%within%` |

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1.  What does `ymd("2026-02-30")` return, and why?
2.  Use `floor_date()` to count the number of rows per ISO week in the `flights` data.
3.  A meeting is scheduled for 09:00 in New York on the 4th of every month in 2027. Write code that lists the corresponding local times in Berlin.  Which months are unusual, and why?

    ```{r}
    #| eval: false
    #| code-fold: true
    meetings <- ymd_hm("2027-01-04 09:00", tz = "America/New_York") + months(0:11)
    with_tz(meetings, "Europe/Berlin")
    ```

{{< pagebreak >}}

## Summary

Dates and times are hard because the rules for them were made by people, not by mathematicians.^[And by politicians, who change the daylight saving rules more often than you'd think.] lubridate hides most of the complexity, but it can't hide all of it -- always check the time zone of your data.

title: "Customer churn analysis"
author: "Data Science Team"
date: "`r format(Sys.Date(), '%d %B %Y')`"
output:
  html_document:
    toc: true
    toc_float: true
    theme: flatly
    code_folding: hide

params:
  cutoff_date: "2026-06-30"
editor_options:

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5)
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
churn <- read_csv("data/churn.csv")
```

## Background

Churn has increased steadily since Q3 2025. This report looks at which customer segments drive the increase, e.g. small business customers on monthly plans, and whether the price change in March had a measurable effect. All figures exclude trial accounts, i.e. accounts that never made a payment.

The analysis was requested by Dr. Patel (VP Customer Success) after the board meeting on 14 May.  It follows the methodology agreed with the finance team in 2024, which defines a churned customer as one whose subscription ended and was not renewed within 30 days. Customers who downgraded, as opposed to cancelling, are not counted as churned.

## Data

We have `r nrow(churn)` customers in the dataset, of whom `r sum(churn$churned)` churned before `r params$cutoff_date`. That is a churn rate of `r scales::percent(mean(churn$churned), accuracy = 0.1)`. The data come from the billing system (Stripe) and the CRM (HubSpot); see the appendix for the join logic.

```{r churn-by-plan, fig.cap="Churn rate by plan type and billing interval."}
churn %>%
  group_by(plan, interval) %>%
  summarise(rate = mean(churned), n = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(plan, rate, fill = interval)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent)
```

## Findings

1. Monthly plans churn about three times as often as annual plans. This is unsurprising and in line with industry benchmarks (approx. 3--5% monthly vs. 1% for annual).
2. The March price change did not increase churn among existing customers. It did, however, reduce conversion from trial to paid by roughly 2 percentage points, cf. the dashboard maintained by Mr. Okafor's team.
3. Customers who contacted support at least twice in their first month churn at nearly double the base rate. We think this is the most actionable finding, as it points to onboarding problems rather than to pricing.

## Next steps

We recommend (a) a targeted onboarding campaign for monthly customers, (b) an experiment offering a discount for switching to annual billing, and (c) a deeper dive into the support tickets.  Questions to the team at ds-team@example.com.

```{r setup}
library(tidyclean)
```

tidyclean provides a handful of functions for the boring first 20 minutes of every analysis: fixing column names, trimming whitespace, converting obvious types and flagging duplicates.

## Cleaning column names

```{r}
df <- data.frame(`First Name` = c("Ada", "Grace"), `AGE (years)` = c(36, 85), check.names = FALSE)
clean_names(df)
```

## Trimming whitespace

`trim_all()` trims leading and trailing whitespace from all character columns and, optionally, squishes internal runs of whitespace into a single space:

```{r}
x <- data.frame(name = c("  Ada ", "Grace   Hopper"))
trim_all(x, squish = TRUE)
```

## Guessing types
`guess_types()` is a thin wrapper around `readr::type_convert()` with a few extra rules:

* `"yes"`/`"no"` and `"Y"`/`"N"` become logicals
* numbers with thousands separators (`"1,234"`) become numerics
* ISO 8601 dates become `Date`s

| input | output |
|---|---|
| `"yes"` | `TRUE` |
|`"1,234"`|`1234`|
| `"2026-01-31"` | `as.Date("2026-01-31")` |

See `vignette("advanced", package = "tidyclean")` for the full list of rules and how to add your own.

# Methods {#methods}

## Study area

Fieldwork was carried out in the Yorkshire Dales National Park, U.K., between April 2023 and September 2024. The study area covers approx. 120 km² of upland grassland, blanket bog and limestone pavement, at altitudes between 250 and 700 m a.s.l. Mean annual precipitation at the nearest Met Office station (Malham Tarn) was 1,600 mm over the study period.

Sites were selected using a stratified random design, i.e. the study area was first divided into strata by habitat type and altitude band, and sites were then drawn at random within each stratum (Fig. \@ref(fig:map)). Sites that turned out to be inaccessible, e.g. because the landowner declined permission, were replaced by the next site on the randomised list.

```{r map, fig.cap="Map of the study area showing the 48 sampling sites, coloured by habitat stratum."}
plot_site_map(sites)
```

## Vegetation surveys

At each site we recorded the percentage cover of all vascular plant species in five 1 × 1 m quadrats, following the protocol of @rodwell2006. Nomenclature follows @stace2019. Species that could not be identified in the field were collected and identified later by Dr. M. Brown at the University herbarium.

Bryophytes were recorded as a single group, as identifying them to species level was beyond the scope (and, frankly, the expertise) of this study. Cf. Section \@ref(limitations) for a discussion of how this may have affected the diversity estimates.

## Statistical analysis

All analyses were carried out in R `r getRversion()` [@rcore2024]. Species richness was modelled with a generalised linear mixed model (GLMM) with a Poisson error distribution and site as a random effect, using **lme4** [@bates2015]. Overdispersion was checked with the **DHARMa** package [@hartig2022]; where present, we refitted the model with a negative binomial distribution, i.e. using `glmer.nb()`.

Model selection followed an information-theoretic approach [@burnham2002]: we fitted all candidate models and ranked them by AICc. Models within 2 AICc units of the best model were considered to have substantial support. In total, `r nrow(candidate_models)` candidate models were fitted.

### Limitations {#limitations}

The sampling was restricted to the growing season (Apr.--Sept.), so early-flowering species may be under-represented. Further, the 2023 season was unusually dry, e.g. July rainfall was 40% below the long-term average, which may have affected cover estimates for drought-sensitive species.

---
title: "A note on the reproducibility of published R analyses"
author:
- Alex Example^[Department of Statistics, Example University, alex@example.edu]
- Sam Sample
date: "Draft of `r Sys.Date()`"
abstract: "We attempted to reproduce the main results of 60 articles published in two applied statistics journals in 2023, using only the code and data provided by the authors. In 22 cases (37%) we obtained the published numbers without modification; in a further 19 cases (32%) minor changes were needed, typically to file paths or package versions."
output:
  pdf_document:
    number_sections: yes
    citation_package: natbib
    latex_engine: xelatex
    extra_dependencies: ["booktabs", "float"]
fontsize: 11pt
geometry: margin=2.5cm
bibliography: references.bib
biblio-style: apalike
editor_options:
  markdown:
    wrap: sentence
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.pos = "H")
library(tidyverse); library(kableExtra)
results <- readRDS("data/reproduction_results.rds")
```

# Introduction

Reproducibility, i.e. obtaining the same results from the same data and code, is a minimal standard for computational research [@peng2011]. It is weaker than replicability, which requires new data. Despite the increasing availability of code, several studies have found that a majority of published analyses cannot be reproduced without help from the original authors [@stodden2018; @trisovic2022].

Journals have responded in different ways. Some, e.g. the *Journal of Statistical Software*, have long required code; others merely encourage it. Since 2022, the two journals in our sample have required authors to deposit code and data, except where data are confidential.

# Methods

We drew a random sample of 60 articles from the `r nrow(results)` eligible articles published in 2023. Two of us (A.E. and S.S.) independently attempted to reproduce the main result of each article, defined as the first numerical result reported in the abstract. Each reproduction was capped at eight hours of work. We used R 4.3.2 and the package versions current on 1 Jan. 2024 unless the authors specified otherwise, e.g. via `renv.lock`.

```{r tab-outcomes}
results %>%
  count(outcome) %>%
  mutate(pct = scales::percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = 1)) %>%
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, caption = "Reproduction outcomes.", col.names = c("Outcome", "n", "%")) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position")
```

# Results

Table \ref{tab:tab-outcomes} summarises the outcomes. The most common obstacles were missing data files (n = 9), undocumented dependencies (n = 7), and hard-coded absolute paths, e.g. `C:/Users/...` (n = 6). Interestingly, articles that used **renv** or Docker were not significantly more likely to reproduce (Fisher's exact test, p = 0.21), though the sample was small.

# Discussion

Our results are broadly consistent with those of @trisovic2022, who found that a large share of R scripts deposited in a public data repository failed to run without error. We stress that a failure to reproduce does not imply that the published results are wrong. In most cases we believe the problems were mundane, e.g. a file was renamed after the analysis was run.

df <- data.frame(`First Name` = c("Ada", "Grace"), `AGE (years)` = c(36, 85), check.names = FALSE)
clean_names(df)
```

## Trimming whitespace

`trim_all()` trims leading and trailing whitespace from all character columns and, optionally, squishes internal runs of whitespace into a single space:

```{r}
x <- data.frame(name = c("  Ada ", "Grace   Hopper"))
trim_all(x, squish = TRUE)
```

## Guessing types
`guess_types()` is a thin wrapper around `readr::type_convert()` with a few extra rules:

* `"yes"`/`"no"` and `"Y"`/`"N"` become logicals
* numbers with thousands separators (`"1,234"`) become numerics
* ISO 8601 dates become `Date`s

| input | output |
|---|---|
| `"yes"` | `TRUE` |
|`"1,234"`|`1234`|
| `"2026-01-31"` | `as.Date("2026-01-31")` |

See `vignette("advanced", package = "tidyclean")` for the full list of rules and how to add your own.

# Methods {#methods}

## Study area

Fieldwork was carried out in the Yorkshire Dales National Park, U.K., between April 2023 and September 2024. The study area covers approx. 120 km² of upland grassland, blanket bog and limestone pavement, at altitudes between 250 and 700 m a.s.l. Mean annual precipitation at the nearest Met Office station (Malham Tarn) was 1,600 mm over the study period.

Sites were selected using a stratified random design, i.e. the study area was first divided into strata by habitat type and altitude band, and sites were then drawn at random within each stratum (Fig. \@ref(fig:map)). Sites that turned out to be inaccessible, e.g. because the landowner declined permission, were replaced by the next site on the randomised list.

```{r map, fig.cap="Map of the study area showing the 48 sampling sites, coloured by habitat stratum."}
plot_site_map(sites)
```

## Vegetation surveys

At each site we recorded the percentage cover of all vascular plant species in five 1 × 1 m quadrats, following the protocol of @rodwell2006. Nomenclature follows @stace2019. Species that could not be identified in the field were collected and identified later by Dr. M. Brown at the University herbarium.

Bryophytes were recorded as a single group, as identifying them to species level was beyond the scope (and, frankly, the expertise) of this study. Cf. Section \@ref(limitations) for a discussion of how this may have affected the diversity estimates.

## Statistical analysis

All analyses were carried out in R `r getRversion()` [@rcore2024]. Species richness was modelled with a generalised linear mixed model (GLMM) with a Poisson error distribution and site as a random effect, using **lme4** [@bates2015]. Overdispersion was checked with the **DHARMa** package [@hartig2022]; where present, we refitted the model with a negative binomial distribution, i.e. using `glmer.nb()`.

Model selection followed an information-theoretic approach [@burnham2002]: we fitted all candidate models and ranked them by AICc. Models within 2 AICc units of the best model were considered to have substantial support. In total, `r nrow(candidate_models)` candidate models were fitted.

### Limitations {#limitations}

The sampling was restricted to the growing season (Apr.--Sept.), so early-flowering species may be under-represented. Further, the 2023 season was unusually dry, e.g. July rainfall was 40% below the long-term average, which may have affected cover estimates for drought-sensitive species.

# Introduction

Reproducibility, i.e. obtaining the same results from the same data and code, is a minimal standard for computational research [@peng2011]. It is weaker than replicability, which requires new data. Despite the increasing availability of code, several studies have found that a majority of published analyses cannot be reproduced without help from the original authors [@stodden2018; @trisovic2022].

Journals have responded in different ways. Some, e.g. the *Journal of Statistical Software*, have long required code; others merely encourage it. Since 2022, the two journals in our sample have required authors to deposit code and data, except where data are confidential.

# Methods

We drew a random sample of 60 articles from the `r nrow(results)` eligible articles published in 2023. Two of us (A.E. and S.S.) independently attempted to reproduce the main result of each article, defined as the first numerical result reported in the abstract. Each reproduction was capped at eight hours of work. We used R 4.3.2 and the package versions current on 1 Jan. 2024 unless the authors specified otherwise, e.g. via `renv.lock`.

```{r tab-outcomes}
results %>%
  count(outcome) %>%
  mutate(pct = scales::percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = 1)) %>%
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, caption = "Reproduction outcomes.", col.names = c("Outcome", "n", "%")) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position")
```

# Results

Table \ref{tab:tab-outcomes} summarises the outcomes. The most common obstacles were missing data files (n = 9), undocumented dependencies (n = 7), and hard-coded absolute paths, e.g. `C:/Users/...` (n = 6). Interestingly, articles that used **renv** or Docker were not significantly more likely to reproduce (Fisher's exact test, p = 0.21), though the sample was small.

# Discussion

Our results are broadly consistent with those of @trisovic2022, who found that a large share of R scripts deposited in a public data repository failed to run without error. We stress that a failure to reproduce does not imply that the published results are wrong. In most cases we believe the problems were mundane, e.g. a file was renamed after the analysis was run.

#| title: Train churn model
#| description:   Gradient-boosted trees on the customer churn dataset, with
#|   early stopping and a held-out test set.
#| tags: [ml,  churn, "xgboost" ]
#| params:
#|     learning_rate: 0.05
#|     max_depth: 6
#|     n_estimators:    2000
#|     early_stopping_rounds: 50
#| data:
#|   train: data/churn_train.parquet
#|   test:  "data/churn_test.parquet"
#| outputs:
#| - models/churn_xgb.json
#| - reports/metrics.json
"""Train a gradient-boosted churn model.

Usage::

    python train_model.py --train data/churn_train.parquet --test data/churn_test.parquet
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import logging
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd
import xgboost as xgb
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score, roc_auc_score

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)

FEATURES = [
    "tenure_months",
    "monthly_charges",
    "support_tickets_30d",
    "plan_annual",
    "seats",
]


@dataclass
class Params:
    learning_rate: float = 0.05
    max_depth: int = 6
    n_estimators: int = 2000
    early_stopping_rounds: int = 50
    extra: dict[str, float] = field(default_factory=dict)


def load(path: str | Path) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.Series]:
    df = pd.read_parquet(path)
    return df[FEATURES], df["churned"].astype(int)


def train(params: Params, train_path: Path, test_path: Path) -> dict[str, float]:
    X_train, y_train = load(train_path)
    X_test, y_test = load(test_path)

    model = xgb.XGBClassifier(
        learning_rate=params.learning_rate,
        max_depth=params.max_depth,
        n_estimators=params.n_estimators,
        early_stopping_rounds=params.early_stopping_rounds,
        eval_metric="aucpr",
        **params.extra,
    )
    model.fit(X_train, y_train, eval_set=[(X_test, y_test)], verbose=100)

    proba = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
    metrics = {
        "roc_auc": roc_auc_score(y_test, proba),
        "pr_auc": average_precision_score(y_test, proba),
        "best_iteration": int(model.best_iteration),
    }
    Path("models").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    model.save_model("models/churn_xgb.json")
    return metrics


def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.splitlines()[0])
    parser.add_argument("--train", type=Path, default=Path("data/churn_train.parquet"))
    parser.add_argument("--test", type=Path, default=Path("data/churn_test.parquet"))
    parser.add_argument("--learning-rate", type=float, default=0.05)
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)

    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s")
    metrics = train(Params(learning_rate=args.learning_rate), args.train, args.test)
    log.info("metrics: %s", metrics)
    Path("reports").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    Path("reports/metrics.json").write_text(json.dumps(metrics, indent=2))
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

"""Build the weekly status report e-mail."""
from __future__ import annotations

import datetime as dt
from string import Template

# fmt: markdown
# Weekly report template
# ======================
#
# The template below is rendered with `string.Template`, so placeholders look like `$name` or `${name}`.
# Keep it short: the e-mail is read on phones.
#  * one heading
#  * at most five bullet points
# * a link to the dashboard

# fmt: markdown
TEMPLATE = '''
## Weekly status -- ${week}

Hi team,

here is the summary for the week of ${week_start} to ${week_end}:

- **Deploys:** ${deploys} (${failed_deploys} rolled back)
- **Incidents:** ${incidents}
- **Error budget remaining:** ${budget}%

Full details are on the [dashboard](${dashboard_url}).

Thanks,
the platform team
'''


def week_bounds(today: dt.date) -> tuple[dt.date, dt.date]:
    start = today - dt.timedelta(days=today.weekday())
    return start, start + dt.timedelta(days=6)


def render(stats: dict[str, object], today: dt.date | None = None) -> str:
    today = today or dt.date.today()
    start, end = week_bounds(today)
    return Template(TEMPLATE).substitute(
        week=today.isocalendar().week,
        week_start=start.isoformat(),
        week_end=end.isoformat(),
        dashboard_url="https://grafana.example.com/d/platform-weekly",
        **stats,
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(render({"deploys": 42, "failed_deploys": 1, "incidents": 0, "budget": 87.5}))

"""Nightly ETL: extract orders from Postgres, transform, load into the warehouse."""

import os
from datetime import date, timedelta

import psycopg
import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.parquet as pq

DSN = os.environ.get("ORDERS_DSN", "postgresql://readonly@orders-db:5432/orders")


#| step: extract
#| depends_on: []
#| timeout: 30m
#| tags:
#|     - io
#|     - postgres
def extract(day: date) -> pa.Table:
    query = """
        SELECT id, customer_id, total_cents, currency, created_at
        FROM orders
        WHERE created_at >= %(start)s AND created_at < %(end)s
    """
    with psycopg.connect(DSN) as conn, conn.cursor() as cur:
        cur.execute(query, {"start": day, "end": day + timedelta(days=1)})
        rows = cur.fetchall()
        names = [d.name for d in cur.description]
    return pa.Table.from_pylist([dict(zip(names, r)) for r in rows])


#| step: transform
#| depends_on: [extract]
#| description: >
#|   Convert cents to decimal amounts, normalise currency codes
#|   and drop test orders (customer_id < 1000).
def transform(table: pa.Table) -> pa.Table:
    import pyarrow.compute as pc

    table = table.filter(pc.greater_equal(table["customer_id"], 1000))
    amount = pc.divide(pc.cast(table["total_cents"], pa.float64()), 100.0)
    return table.append_column("amount", amount).drop(["total_cents"])


#| step: load
#| depends_on: [ transform ]
#| outputs:
#|   - path: "s3://acme-warehouse/orders/dt={{ ds }}/part-0.parquet"
#|     format: parquet
#|     compression:   zstd
def load(table: pa.Table, day: date) -> str:
    path = f"s3://acme-warehouse/orders/dt={day.isoformat()}/part-0.parquet"
    pq.write_table(table, path, compression="zstd")
    return path


if __name__ == "__main__":
    yesterday = date.today() - timedelta(days=1)
    print(load(transform(extract(yesterday)), yesterday))

import pandas as pd

# A/B test explorer
Pick an experiment on the left to see its results.  Conversion rates are computed per *visitor*, not per session; the credible intervals come from a Beta(1, 1) prior -- see the [methodology page](https://wiki.example.com/ab-testing/methodology) for details.
"""

    return pd.read_parquet("s3://acme-analytics/experiments/latest.parquet")


def sidebar(df: pd.DataFrame) -> str:
    # fmt: markdown
    # **How to use the filters**
    #
    # 1. pick an experiment
    # 2. optionally restrict to a country
    #    (applies to both variants)
    st.sidebar.header("Filters")
    experiment = st.sidebar.selectbox("Experiment", sorted(df.experiment.unique()))
    return experiment


def main() -> None:
    st.markdown(INTRO)
    df = load_experiments()
    experiment = sidebar(df)
    sub = df[df.experiment == experiment]

    col1, col2 = st.columns(2)
    for col, variant in zip((col1, col2), ("A", "B")):
        v = sub[sub.variant == variant]
        col.metric(f"Variant {variant}", f"{v.converted.mean():.2%}", help=f"{len(v):,} visitors")

    # fmt: markdown
    footnote = """
    ---
    _Data refreshed every 10 minutes._ Questions? Ask in #analytics.
    """
    st.caption(footnote)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Train a gradient-boosted churn model.

Usage::

    python train_model.py --train data/churn_train.parquet --test data/churn_test.parquet
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import logging
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd
import xgboost as xgb
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score, roc_auc_score

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)

FEATURES = [
    "tenure_months",
    "monthly_charges",
    "support_tickets_30d",
    "plan_annual",
    "seats",
]


@dataclass
class Params:
    learning_rate: float = 0.05
    max_depth: int = 6
    n_estimators: int = 2000
    early_stopping_rounds: int = 50
    extra: dict[str, float] = field(default_factory=dict)


def load(path: str | Path) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.Series]:
    df = pd.read_parquet(path)
    return df[FEATURES], df["churned"].astype(int)


def train(params: Params, train_path: Path, test_path: Path) -> dict[str, float]:
    X_train, y_train = load(train_path)
    X_test, y_test = load(test_path)

    model = xgb.XGBClassifier(
        learning_rate=params.learning_rate,
        max_depth=params.max_depth,
        n_estimators=params.n_estimators,
        early_stopping_rounds=params.early_stopping_rounds,
        eval_metric="aucpr",
        **params.extra,
    )
    model.fit(X_train, y_train, eval_set=[(X_test, y_test)], verbose=100)

    proba = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
    metrics = {
        "roc_auc": roc_auc_score(y_test, proba),
        "pr_auc": average_precision_score(y_test, proba),
        "best_iteration": int(model.best_iteration),
    }
    Path("models").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    model.save_model("models/churn_xgb.json")
    return metrics


def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.splitlines()[0])
    parser.add_argument("--train", type=Path, default=Path("data/churn_train.parquet"))
    parser.add_argument("--test", type=Path, default=Path("data/churn_test.parquet"))
    parser.add_argument("--learning-rate", type=float, default=0.05)
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)

    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s")
    metrics = train(Params(learning_rate=args.learning_rate), args.train, args.test)
    log.info("metrics: %s", metrics)
    Path("reports").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    Path("reports/metrics.json").write_text(json.dumps(metrics, indent=2))
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

from __future__ import annotations

import datetime as dt
from string import Template

# fmt: markdown
# Weekly report template
# ======================
#
# The template below is rendered with `string.Template`, so placeholders look like `$name` or `${name}`.
# Keep it short: the e-mail is read on phones.
#  * one heading
#  * at most five bullet points
# * a link to the dashboard

# fmt: markdown
TEMPLATE = '''
## Weekly status -- ${week}

Hi team,

here is the summary for the week of ${week_start} to ${week_end}:

- **Deploys:** ${deploys} (${failed_deploys} rolled back)
- **Incidents:** ${incidents}
- **Error budget remaining:** ${budget}%

Full details are on the [dashboard](${dashboard_url}).

Thanks,
the platform team
'''


def week_bounds(today: dt.date) -> tuple[dt.date, dt.date]:
    start = today - dt.timedelta(days=today.weekday())
    return start, start + dt.timedelta(days=6)


def render(stats: dict[str, object], today: dt.date | None = None) -> str:
    today = today or dt.date.today()
    start, end = week_bounds(today)
    return Template(TEMPLATE).substitute(
        week=today.isocalendar().week,
        week_start=start.isoformat(),
        week_end=end.isoformat(),
        dashboard_url="https://grafana.example.com/d/platform-weekly",
        **stats,
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(render({"deploys": 42, "failed_deploys": 1, "incidents": 0, "budget": 87.5}))

"""Nightly ETL: extract orders from Postgres, transform, load into the warehouse."""

import os
from datetime import date, timedelta

import psycopg
import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.parquet as pq

DSN = os.environ.get("ORDERS_DSN", "postgresql://readonly@orders-db:5432/orders")


#| step: extract
#| depends_on: []
#| timeout: 30m
#| tags:
#|     - io
#|     - postgres
def extract(day: date) -> pa.Table:
    query = """
        SELECT id, customer_id, total_cents, currency, created_at
        FROM orders
        WHERE created_at >= %(start)s AND created_at < %(end)s
    """
    with psycopg.connect(DSN) as conn, conn.cursor() as cur:
        cur.execute(query, {"start": day, "end": day + timedelta(days=1)})
        rows = cur.fetchall()
        names = [d.name for d in cur.description]
    return pa.Table.from_pylist([dict(zip(names, r)) for r in rows])


#| step: transform
#| depends_on: [extract]
#| description: >
#|   Convert cents to decimal amounts, normalise currency codes
#|   and drop test orders (customer_id < 1000).
def transform(table: pa.Table) -> pa.Table:
    import pyarrow.compute as pc

    table = table.filter(pc.greater_equal(table["customer_id"], 1000))
    amount = pc.divide(pc.cast(table["total_cents"], pa.float64()), 100.0)
    return table.append_column("amount", amount).drop(["total_cents"])


#| step: load
#| depends_on: [ transform ]
#| outputs:
#|   - path: "s3://acme-warehouse/orders/dt={{ ds }}/part-0.parquet"
#|     format: parquet
#|     compression:   zstd
def load(table: pa.Table, day: date) -> str:
    path = f"s3://acme-warehouse/orders/dt={day.isoformat()}/part-0.parquet"
    pq.write_table(table, path, compression="zstd")
    return path


if __name__ == "__main__":
    yesterday = date.today() - timedelta(days=1)
    print(load(transform(extract(yesterday)), yesterday))

#' Clean column names
#'
#' Converts column names to `snake_case`, removes accents and replaces
#' any run of non-alphanumeric characters with a single underscore.  Duplicate names get a numeric suffix (`x`, `x_2`, `x_3`, ...).
#'
#' @param df A data frame.
#' @param case One of `"snake"` (default), `"camel"` or `"upper"`.
#' @return `df` with cleaned names.
#' @export
#' @examples
#' df <- data.frame(`First Name` = 1, `AGE (years)` = 2, check.names = FALSE)
#' clean_names(df)
clean_names <- function(df, case = c("snake", "camel", "upper")) {
  case <- match.arg(case)
  nms <- iconv(names(df), to = "ASCII//TRANSLIT")
  nms <- tolower(gsub("[^A-Za-z0-9]+", "_", nms))
  nms <- gsub("^_|_$", "", nms)
  nms <- make.unique(nms, sep = "_")
  names(df) <- switch(case,
    snake = nms,
    camel = gsub("_(\\w)", "\\U\\1", nms, perl = TRUE),
    upper = toupper(nms)
  )
  df
}

#' Trim whitespace in all character columns
#'
#' @param df A data frame.
#' @param squish If `TRUE`, also collapse internal runs of whitespace into a single space,
#'   like [stringr::str_squish()].
#'
#' @return A data frame of the same shape as `df`.
#' @export
#'
#' @seealso [clean_names()], [guess_types()]
trim_all <- function(df, squish = FALSE) {
  chr <- vapply(df, is.character, logical(1))
  df[chr] <- lapply(df[chr], function(x) {
    x <- trimws(x)
    if (squish) gsub("\\s+", " ", x) else x
  })
  df
}

#' Flag duplicated rows
#'
#' @description
#' Adds a logical column `.dup` that is `TRUE` for every row that is a duplicate of an earlier row, considering only the columns in `cols`.
#'
#' * Missing values are treated as equal to each other.
#' * The first occurrence is **not** flagged.
#'
#' @param df A data frame.
#' @param cols <[`tidy-select`][dplyr::dplyr_tidy_select]> Columns to compare. Defaults to all columns.
#' @returns `df` with an extra column `.dup`.
#' @export
flag_duplicates <- function(df, cols = dplyr::everything()) {
  sel <- tidyselect::eval_select(rlang::enquo(cols), df)
  df$.dup <- duplicated(df[sel])
  df
}

`%||%` <- function(x, y) if (is.null(x)) y else x

# fmt: markdown
# Plot helpers
# ============
#
# Every function in this file returns a **ggplot object** so callers can keep adding layers.  Colours come from `palette_acme()`; never hard-code hex values in plotting code, because the brand palette changed twice in 2025 and it was a pain to update.
#
# * `plot_trend()` -- line chart with an optional target line
# * `plot_share()` -- stacked bar chart of shares
#   (percent scale)

library(ggplot2)

#' ACME colour palette
#'
#' @param n Number of colours.
#' @return A character vector of hex colours.
#' @noRd
palette_acme <- function(n = 5) {
  cols <- c("#1b3a5c", "#e4572e", "#29a19c", "#f3a712", "#a8c686")
  rep_len(cols, n)
}

#' Line chart with an optional target line
#'
#' @param data A data frame with columns `date` and `value`, and optionally `group`.
#' @param target Optional numeric target, drawn as a dashed horizontal line.
#' @param title Plot title.
#' @return A [ggplot2::ggplot()] object.
#' @export
plot_trend <- function(data, target = NULL, title = NULL) {
  has_group <- "group" %in% names(data)
  p <- ggplot(data, aes(date, value, colour = if (has_group) group else NULL)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = palette_acme(), guide = if (has_group) "legend" else "none") +
    labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
  if (!is.null(target)) {
    p <- p + geom_hline(yintercept = target, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40")
  }
  p
}

#' Stacked bar chart of shares
#'
#' @inheritParams plot_trend
#' @param x,fill Column names (strings).
#' @export
plot_share <- function(data, x, fill, title = NULL) {
  ggplot(data, aes(.data[[x]], fill = .data[[fill]])) +
    geom_bar(position = "fill") +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = palette_acme(length(unique(data[[fill]])))) +
    labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = "Share", fill = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
}

#' Clean column names
#'
#' Converts column names to `snake_case`, removes accents and replaces
#' any run of non-alphanumeric characters with a single underscore.  Duplicate names get a numeric suffix (`x`, `x_2`, `x_3`, ...).
#'
#' @param df A data frame.
#' @param case One of `"snake"` (default), `"camel"` or `"upper"`.
#' @return `df` with cleaned names.
#' @export
#' @examples
#' df <- data.frame(`First Name` = 1, `AGE (years)` = 2, check.names = FALSE)
#' clean_names(df)
clean_names <- function(df, case = c("snake", "camel", "upper")) {
  case <- match.arg(case)
  nms <- iconv(names(df), to = "ASCII//TRANSLIT")
  nms <- tolower(gsub("[^A-Za-z0-9]+", "_", nms))
  nms <- gsub("^_|_$", "", nms)
  nms <- make.unique(nms, sep = "_")
  names(df) <- switch(case,
    snake = nms,
    camel = gsub("_(\\w)", "\\U\\1", nms, perl = TRUE),
    upper = toupper(nms)
  )
  df
}

#' Trim whitespace in all character columns
#'
#' @param df A data frame.
#' @param squish If `TRUE`, also collapse internal runs of whitespace into a single space,
#'   like [stringr::str_squish()].
#'
#' @return A data frame of the same shape as `df`.
#' @export
#'
#' @seealso [clean_names()], [guess_types()]
trim_all <- function(df, squish = FALSE) {
  chr <- vapply(df, is.character, logical(1))
  df[chr] <- lapply(df[chr], function(x) {
    x <- trimws(x)
    if (squish) gsub("\\s+", " ", x) else x
  })
  df
}

#' Flag duplicated rows
#'
#' @description
#' Adds a logical column `.dup` that is `TRUE` for every row that is a duplicate of an earlier row, considering only the columns in `cols`.
#'
#' * Missing values are treated as equal to each other.
#' * The first occurrence is **not** flagged.
#'
#' @param df A data frame.
#' @param cols <[`tidy-select`][dplyr::dplyr_tidy_select]> Columns to compare. Defaults to all columns.
#' @returns `df` with an extra column `.dup`.
#' @export
flag_duplicates <- function(df, cols = dplyr::everything()) {
  sel <- tidyselect::eval_select(rlang::enquo(cols), df)
  df$.dup <- duplicated(df[sel])
  df
}

# internal helper, not exported
`%||%` <- function(x, y) if (is.null(x)) y else x

#' ---
#' title: "Weekly sales summary"
#' author: "Analytics"
#' output:
#'   html_document:
#'     toc: true
#' ---

#' This report is generated with `knitr::spin()` from a plain R script.
#' Lines starting with `#'` are Markdown, everything else is R code.
#' It's a nice way to keep a script runnable *and* get a readable report out of it, without maintaining a separate .Rmd file.

#+ setup, include=FALSE
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
sales <- readr::read_csv("data/sales_weekly.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

#' ## Totals
#'
#' Revenue by region for the last week:

#| label: totals
#| echo: false
sales |>
  filter(week == max(week)) |>
  count(region, wt = revenue, name = "revenue") |>
  arrange(desc(revenue)) |>
  knitr::kable(format.args = list(big.mark = ","))

#' ## Trend
#'
#' * dashed line = target
#' * shaded area =  80% prediction interval from last quarter's forecast

#| label: fig-trend
#| fig-cap: "Weekly revenue vs. target"
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig.height: 4
ggplot(sales, aes(week, revenue, colour = region)) +

#' Generated on `r Sys.time()`.

# Text snippets for the automated monthly report e-mail.
# The Markdown is converted to HTML with commonmark::markdown_html() before sending.

library(glue)

# fmt: markdown
intro_md <- r"(
# Monthly report -- {month}

Hello {name},

this is your automated monthly summary.  Numbers are *preliminary* until the finance team closes the books, usually on the 5th business day of the following month.
)"

# fmt: markdown
caveats_md <- r"[
## Caveats
* refunds are attributed to the month of the **refund**, not the original order
* figures in GBP and CHF are converted at the ECB reference rate of the last business day
+ the "Other" region includes test accounts (see issue #212)
]"

# fmt: markdown
footer_md <- R"---(
---
You are receiving this because you are subscribed to the *monthly-report* list.
[Unsubscribe]({unsubscribe_url}) | [Settings](https://reports.example.com/settings)
)---"

# fmt: markdown
disclaimer_md <- "
**Disclaimer:** these figures are generated automatically and have not been audited.
Do not forward this e-mail outside the company.
"

# fmt: markdown
signoff_md <- "Best regards,  \nthe **Analytics** team"

build_report <- function(month, name, unsubscribe_url) {
  paste(
    glue(intro_md),
    caveats_md,
    disclaimer_md,
    glue(footer_md),
    signoff_md,
    sep = "\n\n"
  )
}

send_report <- function(to, ...) {
  html <- commonmark::markdown_html(build_report(...), extensions = TRUE)
  blastula::compose_email(body = blastula::md(html)) |>
    blastula::smtp_send(to = to, from = "reports@example.com", subject = "Monthly report",
                        credentials = blastula::creds_envvar(user = "SMTP_USER", pass_envvar = "SMTP_PASS", host = "smtp.example.com"))
}

# fmt: markdown
# Plot helpers
# ============
#
# Every function in this file returns a **ggplot object** so callers can keep adding layers.  Colours come from `palette_acme()`; never hard-code hex values in plotting code, because the brand palette changed twice in 2025 and it was a pain to update.
#
# * `plot_trend()` -- line chart with an optional target line
# * `plot_share()` -- stacked bar chart of shares
#   (percent scale)

library(ggplot2)

#' ACME colour palette
#'
#' @param n Number of colours.
#' @return A character vector of hex colours.
#' @noRd
palette_acme <- function(n = 5) {
  cols <- c("#1b3a5c", "#e4572e", "#29a19c", "#f3a712", "#a8c686")
  rep_len(cols, n)
}

#' Line chart with an optional target line
#'
#' @param data A data frame with columns `date` and `value`, and optionally `group`.
#' @param target Optional numeric target, drawn as a dashed horizontal line.
#' @param title Plot title.
#' @return A [ggplot2::ggplot()] object.
#' @export
plot_trend <- function(data, target = NULL, title = NULL) {
  has_group <- "group" %in% names(data)
  p <- ggplot(data, aes(date, value, colour = if (has_group) group else NULL)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = palette_acme(), guide = if (has_group) "legend" else "none") +
    labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
  if (!is.null(target)) {
    p <- p + geom_hline(yintercept = target, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40")
  }
  p
}

#' Stacked bar chart of shares
#'
#' @inheritParams plot_trend
#' @param x,fill Column names (strings).
#' @export
plot_share <- function(data, x, fill, title = NULL) {
  ggplot(data, aes(.data[[x]], fill = .data[[fill]])) +
    geom_bar(position = "fill") +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = palette_acme(length(unique(data[[fill]])))) +
    labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = "Share", fill = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
}

26	Fieldwork was carried out in the Yorkshire Dales National Park, U.K., between April 2023 and September 2024. The study area covers approx. 120 km² of upland grassland, blanket bog and limestone pavement, at altitudes between 250 and 700 m a.s.l. Mean annual precipitation at the nearest Met Office station (Malham Tarn) was 1,600 mm over the study period.
27	
28	Sites were selected using a stratified random design, i.e. the study area was first divided into strata by habitat type and altitude band, and sites were then drawn at random within each stratum (Fig. \@ref(fig:map)). Sites that turned out to be inaccessible, e.g. because the landowner declined permission, were replaced by the next site on the randomised list.
29	
30	```{r map, fig.cap="Map of the study area showing the 48 sampling sites, coloured by habitat stratum."}
31	plot_site_map(sites)
32	```
33	
34	## Vegetation surveys  
35	
36	At each site we recorded the percentage cover of all vascular plant species in five 1 × 1 m quadrats, following the protocol of @rodwell2006. Nomenclature follows @stace2019. Species that could not be identified in the field were collected and identified later by Dr. M. Brown at the University herbarium.
37	
38	Bryophytes were recorded as a single group, as identifying them to species level was beyond the scope (and, frankly, the expertise) of this study. Cf. Section \@ref(limitations) for a discussion of how this may have affected the diversity estimates.
39	
40	## Statistical analysis
41	
42	All analyses were carried out in R `r getRversion()` [@rcore2024]. Species richness was modelled with a generalised linear mixed model (GLMM) with a Poisson error distribution and site as a random effect, using **lme4** [@bates2015]. Overdispersion was checked with the **DHARMa** package [@hartig2022]; where present, we refitted the model with a negative binomial distribution, i.e. using `glmer.nb()`.

26	## Background 
27	
28	Churn has increased steadily since Q3 2025. This report looks at which customer segments drive the increase, e.g. small business customers on monthly plans, and whether the price change in March had a measurable effect. All figures exclude trial accounts, i.e. accounts that never made a payment.
29	
30	The analysis was requested by Dr. Patel (VP Customer Success) after the board meeting on 14 May.  It follows the methodology agreed with the finance team in 2024, which defines a churned customer as one whose subscription ended and was not renewed within 30 days. Customers who downgraded, as opposed to cancelling, are not counted as churned.
31	
32	## Data
33	
34	We have `r nrow(churn)` customers in the dataset, of whom `r sum(churn$churned)` churned before `r params$cutoff_date`. That is a churn rate of `r scales::percent(mean(churn$churned), accuracy = 0.1)`. The data come from the billing system (Stripe) and the CRM (HubSpot); see the appendix for the join logic.

3	date: 2026-03-14T09:30:00+01:00
4	draft: false
5	authors: [ "jdoe", 'msmith' ]
6	tags: 
7	  - observability
8	  - opentelemetry

10	summary: >
11	  A year-long migration, three false starts, and one very large Grafana bill.
12	canonical_url: https://engineering.example.com/blog/2026/03/opentelemetry-migration/
13	---
14	
15	When we started the migration in January 2025 we had three different tracing libraries, two metrics
16	pipelines and a logging setup that only one person fully understood. Fourteen months later 
17	every service emits OpenTelemetry, the old collectors are switched off, and our observability bill is
18	down by roughly a third. This post is about the parts that went well, the parts that did not,
19	and the things we would do differently if we started again tomorrow.
20	
21	## Why bother?
22	
23	The short answer is vendor lock-in. The longer answer is that each of our three tracing libraries had its own idea of what a "service name" was, which made cross-team traces nearly useless: a request that went from the storefront through the checkout service into the payment gateway would show up as three disconnected traces in two different tools.
24
